verseByVerse.quote: So we took the land at that time out of the hand of the two kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan, from the Valley of the Arnon to Mount Hermon (the Sidonians call Hermon Sirion, while the Amorites call it Senir), all the cities of the tableland and all Gilead and all Bashan, as far as Salecah and Edrei, cities of the kingdom of Og in Bashan. (For only Og the king of Bashan was left of the remnant of the Rephaim. Behold, his bed was a bed of iron. Is it not in Rabbah of the Ammonites? Nine cubits was its length, and four cubits its breadth, according to the common cubit.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the narrator stops the account for a museum note, and it is a strange and human touch. (For only Og the king of Bashan was left of the remnant of the Rephaim. Behold, his bed was a bed of iron. Is it not in Rabbah of the Ammonites? Nine cubits was its length, and four cubits its breadth, according to the common cubit.)

Nine cubits by four — something over thirteen feet long and six wide. Iron, in an age when iron was rare and costly. And the writer’s aside is almost conversational: is it not in Rabbah? — you can go and look at it; it is on display in the Ammonite capital.

Whether it was a bed or a basalt sarcophagus, the point of recording it is the same. A generation later, the only thing left of the last giant in Canaan was a piece of furniture that tourists could go and stare at. The man who came out at Edrei with an army had become an exhibit.

Scripture does this repeatedly with the things that frighten people. It does not deny that they were frightening; it tells you what became of them. Pharaoh’s chariots are on the sea floor. Og’s bed is in a museum. And the last enemy, the one nobody escapes, is described in the same register: O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting? (1 Cor. 15:55).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–22 — The Land Allotted; ‘The LORD Fights for You’
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses allots the conquered eastern land to Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh, charging their fighting men to cross the Jordan and help their brothers before settling, for the LORD their God fights for them.
verseByVerse.theology: The people of God are one body; no tribe may rest in its own inheritance while brothers still fight for theirs. Victory belongs to the LORD who goes before.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the eastern tribes must fight for their brothers before enjoying their own land. Now: Christians cannot settle into private comfort while the whole body still labors.

verseByVerse.quote: "When we took possession of this land at that time, I gave to the Reubenites and the Gadites the territory beginning at Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, and half the hill country of Gilead with its cities. The rest of Gilead, and all Bashan, the kingdom of Og, that is, all the region of Argob, I gave to the half-tribe of Manasseh. (All that portion of Bashan is called the land of Rephaim. Jair the Manassite took all the region of Argob, that is, Bashan, as far as the border of the Geshurites and the Maacathites, and called the villages after his own name, Havvoth-jair, as it is to this day.) To Machir I gave Gilead, and to the Reubenites and the Gadites I gave the territory from Gilead as far as the Valley of the Arnon, with the middle of the valley as a border, as far over as the river Jabbok, the border of the Ammonites; the Arabah also, with the Jordan as the border, from Chinnereth as far as the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, under the slopes of Pisgah on the east.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The conquered territory is now divided — Reuben and Gad from the Arnon to Gilead, the half-tribe of Manasseh taking Bashan, with the boundaries traced river by river and ridge by ridge.

Six verses of surveying, and the reason they are here is that this is the first land any Israelite has actually owned since Egypt. Four hundred years of slavery, forty years of tents, and now somebody has a deed. The care of the record matches the size of the moment: God’s gifts are not received in a heap but measured out and written down.

Note also what it proves. The generation being addressed is standing on ground it has already been given. Moses is about to ask them to trust God for a country across a river, and the argument in their favour is not theoretical — they can walk out of the assembly and stand on the first instalment.

God very often works that way with his people. The full inheritance is still across the water; there is usually something already in hand as a pledge of it. Paul calls the Spirit exactly that: the guarantee of our inheritance until we acquire possession of it (Eph. 1:14).

verseByVerse.quote: "And I commanded you at that time, saying, 'The LORD your God has given you this land to possess. All your men of valor shall cross over armed before your brothers, the people of Israel. Only your wives, your little ones, and your livestock (I know that you have much livestock) shall remain in the cities that I have given you, until the LORD gives rest to your brothers, as to you, and they also occupy the land that the LORD your God gives them beyond the Jordan. Then each of you may return to his possession which I have given you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The eastern tribes have their land, and immediately Moses attaches the condition. All your men of valor shall cross over armed before your brothers, the people of Israel. Wives, children and livestock stay; the fighting men go over the Jordan, in the front rank, into a war they have nothing left to gain from.

And the term is set by a single word: until the LORD gives rest to your brothers, as to you.

Rest — Hebrew menuchah — is one of the great words of this book, and it means more than the end of fighting. It is the settled state of a people at home: no more marching, no more tents, everybody on his own ground under his own vine. It is what the whole exodus was for.

And nobody gets it early. That is the force of as to you. Reuben and Gad may not enjoy their rest while their brothers are still in the field, because in God’s reckoning the rest is one thing belonging to one people, not a private arrangement each family reaches separately.

Hebrews takes this word and this idea and builds a whole argument on them — there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God (Heb. 4:9) — and keeps the same corporate shape. No Christian arrives home alone. Which is why the command here is not merely military strategy but a description of what it means to belong to the people of God at all: you do not sit down while your brothers are still fighting.

verseByVerse.quote: And I commanded Joshua at that time, 'Your eyes have seen all that the LORD your God has done to these two kings. So will the LORD do to all the kingdoms into which you are crossing. You shall not fear them, for it is the LORD your God who fights for you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses now turns to the man who will take his place, and the charge is short. Your eyes have seen all that the LORD your God has done to these two kings. So will the LORD do to all the kingdoms into which you are crossing. You shall not fear them, for it is the LORD your God who fights for you.

Three moves in two verses, and the order matters.

First, what Joshua has seen: your eyes have seen. Not what he has been told — what he watched happen to Sihon and Og. Second, the inference: so will the LORD do to everything on the other side of the river. Third, the conclusion drawn for the heart: you shall not fear them.

That is how Scripture consistently deals with fear. It does not tell a man to feel braver. It directs him to something God has actually done, in his own past, that he saw with his own eyes, and reasons forward from it. Faith here is not a mood; it is an argument with a memory in the first premise.

And the last clause takes the weight off Joshua entirely: it is the LORD your God who fights for you. He is being handed a nation and a war and told that the outcome does not finally rest on him. Every leader who has lain awake over something too big should notice that this is the last thing Moses says to his successor before he prays about his own death.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–29 — Moses’ Plea Denied: ‘It Is Enough for You’
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses pleads to be allowed to cross over and see the good land, but the LORD refuses, telling him to view it from Pisgah and to commission Joshua, who will lead the people in.
verseByVerse.theology: Even the greatest mediator of the old covenant cannot bring God’s people into the inheritance; God’s ‘no’ to his servant is itself an act of love and a pointer to Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Moses saw the land but could not enter. Now: we trust God’s sovereign ‘no’ to our prayers and rest in the Joshua-Jesus who brings us home.

verseByVerse.quote: "And I pleaded with the LORD at that time, saying, 'O Lord GOD, you have only begun to show your servant your greatness and your mighty hand. For what god is there in heaven or on earth who can do such works and mighty acts as yours? Please let me go over and see the good land beyond the Jordan, that good hill country and Lebanon.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now the most affecting prayer in the Old Testament. And I pleaded with the LORD at that time. The verb is a plea for grace — the word a man uses when he has no claim and asks anyway.

O Lord GOD, you have only begun to show your servant your greatness and your mighty hand.

Stop at that. Moses is a hundred and twenty. He has seen the bush burn, the Nile turn to blood, the sea open, the mountain shake, the glory fill the tent, bread fall out of the sky for forty years, and the face of God as a man speaks to his friend. And he calls it only begun. There is no trace in him of a man who feels he has seen enough, and no sense that long acquaintance with God has dulled the appetite. The oldest believer in Scripture is the hungriest.

Then the request, and it is almost childlike in its simplicity: Please let me go over and see the good land beyond the Jordan, that good hill country and Lebanon.

He does not ask to lead the conquest. He does not ask to be restored to office or to have the sentence at Meribah reversed on the record. He asks to be allowed to cross a river and look at some hills. Forty years of carrying this nation, and what he wants at the end of it is to see the place he has been walking toward.

verseByVerse.quote: But the LORD was angry with me because of you and would not listen to me. And the LORD said to me, 'Enough from you; do not speak to me of this matter again.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the LORD was angry with me because of you and would not listen to me. And the LORD said to me, “Enough from you; do not speak to me of this matter again.”

God says no. And then he tells Moses to stop asking.

There is no way to make that verse comfortable and it should not be attempted. This is the friend of God, praying a request that is humble, modest and good, and the answer is a closed door and an instruction not to knock again.

Anyone who has prayed for years about one thing knows the size of this verse. Scripture does not hide such cases. Paul asked three times for a thorn to be removed and was refused, and told instead My grace is sufficient for you (2 Cor. 12:8–9). David fasted seven days for a child who died anyway (2 Sam. 12:16–18). And the Lord Jesus in Gethsemane asked three times for a cup to pass and drank it (Matt. 26:39–44). No one is exempt, including him.

Two things must be held together, and neither one alone is honest. God’s refusals are real refusals — he does not always give what his own people ask, and pretending otherwise wrecks faith when the answer comes back no. And God’s refusals are not the last word about the person refused.

Because the end of this is not on the far side of the Jordan. Fourteen centuries later, three frightened disciples woke on a mountain in that very country and saw two men talking with Jesus, and one of them was Moses (Luke 9:30–31). He got into the land. He came in through the front door, in glory, in company with the Christ he had been serving — not because the no was reversed, but because it was never the whole account. What God refused him was a view of some hills. What God had in mind for him was standing next to his Son.

verseByVerse.quote: Go up to the top of Pisgah and lift up your eyes westward and northward and southward and eastward, and look at it with your eyes, for you shall not go over this Jordan. But charge Joshua, and encourage and strengthen him, for he shall go over at the head of this people, and he shall put them in possession of the land that you shall see.' So we remained in the valley opposite Beth-peor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The no is not bare. Three things are given with it.

First, a sight: Go up to the top of Pisgah and lift up your eyes westward and northward and southward and eastward, and look at it with your eyes. Four directions — he is to turn right round and take in the whole thing. God will not let him enter and will not let him die without seeing. There is a real kindness in that, and it costs God nothing to withhold; he gives it anyway.

Second, a task: But charge Joshua, and encourage and strengthen him, for he shall go over at the head of this people, and he shall put them in possession of the land that you shall see.

Read that last phrase slowly. The land that you shall see. Moses’ final assignment is to strengthen the man who will do the thing he has just been forbidden to do, in the country he will only look at. That is asked of him, and there is no hint anywhere in the book that he resented it. His last months are spent making his successor braver.

Third, and easily missed, the location: So we remained in the valley opposite Beth-peor. Beth-peor. That is the shadow of chapter 25 of Numbers — the place of the plague, where twenty-four thousand died over Baal of Peor. The whole of Deuteronomy is preached from a valley facing the site of Israel’s worst failure, and the entire book is a plea not to do it again.

And when Moses dies, God buries him in the valley in the land of Moab opposite Beth-peor (Deut. 34:6). He is laid to rest in sight of the place where his people betrayed their God, by the God who never once betrayed them.

3.theology:
The LORD fights for his people. The defeat of Og, last of the giants, and the charge to Joshua both rest on one truth: “it is the LORD your God who fights for you” (3:22). Faith for the future is built on the remembered faithfulness of the past; the giants behind us assure us of victory over the giants ahead.

The mediator who cannot bring them in. Moses pleads to enter the land and is refused (3:26). The greatest prophet of the old covenant dies outside, for the law cannot carry anyone into the rest. Only Joshua — Yeshua, Jesus — leads the people across the Jordan, foreshadowing the Savior who does what the law could never do.

The love hidden in God’s ‘no.’ God’s firm refusal of Moses’ heartfelt prayer is not cruelty but wisdom and even mercy. The faithful heart, when God says “enough,” stops asking and starts trusting, certain that the One who denies in love sees the whole horizon of glory we cannot yet behold.
3.examples:
Then: Israel watched the last giant fall and the eastern land divided, while Moses climbed Pisgah to see with his eyes a land he would never enter, handing the work to Joshua.

Now: We face our own giants knowing the Lord fights for us, and we point to the “iron beds” — the monuments of past deliverance — when new fears arise. We learn to pray boldly yet submit when God says “enough,” trusting his ‘no’ as love. And we rest our whole hope not in the law that brings us to the border, but in the Joshua-Jesus who carries us across the Jordan into the everlasting inheritance.

4.title: The God Who Speaks: ‘What Great Nation Has a God So Near?’
4.text: <sup>1</sup>"And now, O Israel, listen to the statutes and the rules that I am teaching you, and do them, that you may live, and go in and take possession of the land that the LORD, the God of your fathers, is giving you.<sup>2</sup>You shall not add to the word that I command you, nor take from it, that you may keep the commandments of the LORD your God that I command you.<sup>3</sup>Your eyes have seen what the LORD did at Baal-peor, for the LORD your God destroyed from among you all the men who followed the Baal of Peor.<sup>4</sup>But you who held fast to the LORD your God are all alive today.<sup>5</sup>See, I have taught you statutes and rules, as the LORD my God commanded me, that you should do them in the land that you are entering to take possession of it.<sup>6</sup>Keep them and do them, for that will be your wisdom and your understanding in the sight of the peoples, who, when they hear all these statutes, will say, 'Surely this great nation is a wise and understanding people.'<sup>7</sup>For what great nation is there that has a god so near to it as the LORD our God is to us, whenever we call upon him?<sup>8</sup>And what great nation is there, that has statutes and rules so righteous as all this law that I set before you today?<sup>9</sup>"Only take care, and keep your soul diligently, lest you forget the things that your eyes have seen, and lest they depart from your heart all the days of your life. Make them known to your children and your children's children—<sup>10</sup>how on the day that you stood before the LORD your God at Horeb, the LORD said to me, 'Gather the people to me, that I may let them hear my words, so that they may learn to fear me all the days that they live on the earth, and that they may teach their children so.'<sup>11</sup>And you came near and stood at the foot of the mountain, while the mountain burned with fire to the heart of heaven, wrapped in darkness, cloud, and gloom.<sup>12</sup>Then the LORD spoke to you out of the midst of the fire. You heard the sound of words, but saw no form; there was only a voice.<sup>13</sup>And he declared to you his covenant, which he commanded you to perform, that is, the Ten Commandments, and he wrote them on two tablets of stone.<sup>14</sup>And the LORD commanded me at that time to teach you statutes and rules, that you might do them in the land that you are going over to possess.<sup>15</sup>"Therefore watch yourselves very carefully. Since you saw no form on the day that the LORD spoke to you at Horeb out of the midst of the fire,<sup>16</sup>beware lest you act corruptly by making a carved image for yourselves, in the form of any figure, the likeness of male or female,<sup>17</sup>the likeness of any animal that is on the earth, the likeness of any winged bird that flies in the air,<sup>18</sup>the likeness of anything that creeps on the ground, the likeness of any fish that is in the water under the earth.<sup>19</sup>And beware lest you raise your eyes to heaven, and when you see the sun and the moon and the stars, all the host of heaven, you be drawn away and bow down to them and serve them, things that the LORD your God has allotted to all the peoples under the whole heaven.<sup>20</sup>But the LORD has taken you and brought you out of the iron furnace, out of Egypt, to be a people of his own inheritance, as you are this day.<sup>21</sup>Furthermore, the LORD was angry with me because of you, and he swore that I should not cross the Jordan, and that I should not enter the good land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance.<sup>22</sup>For I must die in this land; I must not go over the Jordan. But you shall go over and take possession of that good land.<sup>23</sup>Take care, lest you forget the covenant of the LORD your God, which he made with you, and make a carved image, the form of anything that the LORD your God has forbidden you.<sup>24</sup>For the LORD your God is a consuming fire, a jealous God.<sup>25</sup>"When you father children and children's children, and have grown old in the land, and you act corruptly by making a carved image in the form of anything, and by doing what is evil in the sight of the LORD your God, so as to provoke him to anger,<sup>26</sup>I call heaven and earth to witness against you today, that you will soon utterly perish from the land that you are going over the Jordan to possess. You will not live long in it, but will be utterly destroyed.<sup>27</sup>And the LORD will scatter you among the peoples, and you will be left few in number among the nations where the LORD will drive you.<sup>28</sup>And there you will serve gods of wood and stone, the work of human hands, that neither see, nor hear, nor eat, nor smell.<sup>29</sup>But from there you will seek the LORD your God and you will find him, if you search after him with all your heart and with all your soul.<sup>30</sup>When you are in tribulation, and all these things come upon you in the latter days, you will return to the LORD your God and obey his voice.<sup>31</sup>For the LORD your God is a merciful God. He will not leave you or destroy you or forget the covenant with your fathers that he swore to them.<sup>32</sup>"For ask now of the days that are past, which were before you, since the day that God created man on the earth, and ask from one end of heaven to the other, whether such a great thing as this has ever happened or was ever heard of.<sup>33</sup>Did any people ever hear the voice of a god speaking out of the midst of the fire, as you have heard, and still live?<sup>34</sup>Or has any god ever attempted to go and take a nation for himself from the midst of another nation, by trials, by signs, by wonders, and by war, by a mighty hand and an outstretched arm, and by great deeds of terror, all of which the LORD your God did for you in Egypt before your eyes?<sup>35</sup>To you it was shown, that you might know that the LORD is God; there is no other besides him.<sup>36</sup>Out of heaven he let you hear his voice, that he might discipline you. And on earth he let you see his great fire, and you heard his words out of the midst of the fire.<sup>37</sup>And because he loved your fathers and chose their offspring after them and brought you out of Egypt with his own presence, by his great power,<sup>38</sup>driving out before you nations greater and mightier than you, to bring you in, to give you their land for an inheritance, as it is this day,<sup>39</sup>know therefore today, and lay it to your heart, that the LORD is God in heaven above and on the earth beneath; there is no other.<sup>40</sup>Therefore you shall keep his statutes and his commandments, which I command you today, that it may go well with you and with your children after you, and that you may prolong your days in the land that the LORD your God is giving you for all time."<sup>41</sup>Then Moses set apart three cities in the east beyond the Jordan,<sup>42</sup>that the manslayer might flee there, anyone who kills his neighbor unintentionally, without being at enmity with him in time past; he may flee to one of these cities and save his life:<sup>43</sup>Bezer in the wilderness on the tableland for the Reubenites, Ramoth in Gilead for the Gadites, and Golan in Bashan for the Manassites.<sup>44</sup>This is the law that Moses set before the people of Israel.<sup>45</sup>These are the testimonies, the statutes, and the rules, which Moses spoke to the people of Israel when they came out of Egypt,<sup>46</sup>beyond the Jordan in the valley opposite Beth-peor, in the land of Sihon the king of the Amorites, who lived at Heshbon, whom Moses and the people of Israel defeated when they came out of Egypt.<sup>47</sup>And they took possession of his land and the land of Og, the king of Bashan, the two kings of the Amorites, who lived to the east beyond the Jordan;<sup>48</sup>from Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, as far as Mount Sirion (that is, Hermon),<sup>49</sup>together with all the Arabah on the east side of the Jordan as far as the Sea of the Arabah, under the slopes of Pisgah.
4.overview:
Chapter 4 is the soaring climax of Moses’ first address — a sermon of breathtaking theological grandeur. Having rehearsed the history, Moses now presses home its meaning: the God who has done all this is utterly unique, and Israel’s response must be wholehearted obedience and exclusive worship. The chapter pulses with the privilege of revelation. No other nation has laws so righteous, a God so near, a redemption so mighty.

At Sinai, Israel “heard the sound of words, but saw no form” (4:12). This is the foundation of the second commandment and of all true worship: God revealed himself by his Word, not by an image. To make an idol is to exchange the living, speaking God for a lifeless thing. Moses warns with fierce tenderness against idolatry, knowing it will be Israel’s besetting sin and the cause of their exile.

Yet even the warning of exile ends in hope: “if from there you seek the LORD your God, you will find him” (4:29). The God who is a “consuming fire” and a “jealous God” is also the merciful God who will not abandon his covenant.

The chapter closes with the appointment of cities of refuge and the great confession that frames all of Israel’s faith: “the LORD is God; there is no other besides him” (4:35, 39). To know this God who speaks, and to obey his Word, is the highest privilege a creature can have.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Privilege of God’s Law and Nearness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses calls Israel to obey God’s statutes without adding or subtracting, for their obedience will display wisdom to the nations and reflect the unique privilege of a God so near and laws so righteous.
verseByVerse.theology: God’s law is a gift and a privilege, not a burden; obedience displays the wisdom of God and the nearness of a God unlike any other.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the nations would marvel at Israel’s wise God. Now: the church’s holy life still commends the gospel and the nearness of God in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, O Israel, listen to the statutes and the rules that I am teaching you, and do them, that you may live, and go in and take possession of the land that the LORD, the God of your fathers, is giving you. You shall not add to the word that I command you, nor take from it, that you may keep the commandments of the LORD your God that I command you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now, O Israel, listen to the statutes and the rules that I am teaching you, and do them, that you may live.

Three chapters of history end, and the sermon turns. And now — everything from here is application. Moses has spent the retrospect showing what God did; from this verse on he shows what Israel is to do about it, and the order is never reversed in Scripture. Grace first, then the response to it.

Note the joint between the two verbs. Listen… and do them, that you may live. Obedience is not the price of life; they are already redeemed, already carried, already standing on the border. It is the path of it. A man does not obey in order to be brought out of Egypt. He obeys because he has been.

Then a sentence that has shaped the whole doctrine of Scripture: You shall not add to the word that I command you, nor take from it.

Both directions are forbidden, and we usually only fear one. Taking away is the obvious sin — cutting out the parts that offend. But adding is named first, and it is the one religious people commit. The Pharisees did not delete the law; they built a fence round it until the fence was heavier than the thing it protected, and the Lord Jesus told them exactly what the result had been: you leave the commandment of God and hold to the tradition of men (Mark 7:8). Every generation of the church adds something and then requires it, and the addition always ends up obscuring what it was meant to guard.

The last book of the Bible closes with the same guard at both ends (Rev. 22:18–19). God’s word is sufficient, and it is finished, and the reverence that will not subtract from it must also refuse to improve it.

verseByVerse.quote: Your eyes have seen what the LORD did at Baal-peor, for the LORD your God destroyed from among you all the men who followed the Baal of Peor. But you who held fast to the LORD your God are all alive today.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your eyes have seen what the LORD did at Baal-peor, for the LORD your God destroyed from among you all the men who followed the Baal of Peor. But you who held fast to the LORD your God are all alive today.

Moses is not arguing from theory. He is pointing across the valley. Beth-peor is in sight of where they are standing, the graves are a few weeks old, and every man listening knows somebody in them. Twenty-four thousand died there (Num. 25:9), and the survivors are the congregation.

Now look at the two verbs that divide the living from the dead. Some followed the Baal of Peor. Others held fast to the LORD.

Take that second phrase in the original. The verb is dabaq — to cling, to stick, to be glued to something. It is the word used of a man and his wife becoming one flesh (Gen. 2:24) and of skin sticking to bone in a famine. It does not describe an opinion. It describes a grip.

And here is the sobering part: the difference between the men in the graves and the men in the congregation was not intelligence, or courage, or upbringing, or how much of the law they knew. They had all come out of Egypt together and eaten the same manna. What separated them was what they were holding on to when the Moabite women came round with an invitation.

Which puts a question to any reader who has watched somebody he respected fall a long way, and wondered how. It was very rarely a failure of information.

verseByVerse.quote: See, I have taught you statutes and rules, as the LORD my God commanded me, that you should do them in the land that you are entering to take possession of it. Keep them and do them, for that will be your wisdom and your understanding in the sight of the peoples, who, when they hear all these statutes, will say, 'Surely this great nation is a wise and understanding people.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Keep them and do them, for that will be your wisdom and your understanding in the sight of the peoples, who, when they hear all these statutes, will say, “Surely this great nation is a wise and understanding people.”

Israel’s obedience is not a private arrangement between her and God. It is evidence, and the nations are the jury.

Consider what the watching world was actually going to see. Not a temple — they had none. Not an army worth the name. Not art, or wealth, or a great city. They would see how these people treated their poor, their slaves, their foreigners, their debtors, their animals and their enemies; and the verdict, Moses says, will be wise.

That is a startling claim about the law. In the ancient world, a nation’s greatness was measured by what it could take. Moses says the surrounding peoples will look at a code that protects the widow, cancels debts every seventh year, forbids moving a boundary stone and orders you to return your enemy’s stray ox — and conclude that these are the people who know how to live.

The same logic governs the church, in the same words: let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven (Matt. 5:16). Nobody is asked to argue the world into the kingdom. They are asked to live in a way that raises the question.

verseByVerse.quote: For what great nation is there that has a god so near to it as the LORD our God is to us, whenever we call upon him? And what great nation is there, that has statutes and rules so righteous as all this law that I set before you today?
verseByVerse.commentary:
And then Moses puts two questions to the nations of the earth, and neither of them has ever been answered.

For what great nation is there that has a god so near to it as the LORD our God is to us, whenever we call upon him? And what great nation is there, that has statutes and rules so righteous as all this law that I set before you today?

Two boasts, and they are the only two Israel had. Not size, not power, not history. Nearness and righteousness.

Take the first. The gods of the ancient world were far off by definition — up a mountain, out at sea, inside a temple that only the priest could enter, reachable through ritual if you knew the correct procedure and could pay for it. Nobody expected their god to be near, and certainly not whenever we call upon him, which puts the initiative in the worshipper’s hands and sets no conditions on the hour or the mood or the man.

Now look at who is saying it. A crowd of former brick-makers standing in a valley with no country, no capital, no king and no temple, being told to name a nation better off than they are. By every measure that a Moabite would have used, they had nothing. And the claim is not that God had made them comfortable. It is that he was close.

Set beside that the sentence written to a church of Gentiles fifteen centuries later — But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ (Eph. 2:13) — and then the invitation that follows from it: Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace (Heb. 4:16). Israel could call whenever she liked, and God was near. The church is nearer, and the distance was closed from his side, at his cost.

There is no other religion on earth whose central boast is proximity. Every other one is about the climb.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–14 — Remember Horeb: The God You Heard but Did Not See
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses urges Israel never to forget the day at Horeb when God spoke from the fire, and to teach it to their children, for they heard a voice but saw no form.
verseByVerse.theology: God reveals himself by his Word, not by visible form; this grounds the prohibition of images and the priority of hearing over seeing in true worship.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel heard God’s voice from the fire. Now: faith comes by hearing the Word, and we teach our children diligently lest grace be forgotten.

verseByVerse.quote: "Only take care, and keep your soul diligently, lest you forget the things that your eyes have seen, and lest they depart from your heart all the days of your life. Make them known to your children and your children's children— how on the day that you stood before the LORD your God at Horeb, the LORD said to me, 'Gather the people to me, that I may let them hear my words, so that they may learn to fear me all the days that they live on the earth, and that they may teach their children so.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Only take care, and keep your soul diligently, lest you forget the things that your eyes have seen, and lest they depart from your heart all the days of your life. Make them known to your children and your children’s children.

The great enemy in Deuteronomy is not persecution or apostasy in the abstract. It is forgetting — and Moses treats it as something that requires active guarding against, not something that merely happens. Keep your soul diligently is the language of a watchman on a wall.

Because memory does not fail suddenly. It thins. The story gets shorter, the details go, the wonder becomes information, and then one day a man finds he can recite what God did for him without any of it touching him. Nobody decides to forget. It is simply what happens to everything that is not deliberately kept.

And notice the timescale in the verse: your children and your children’s children. Moses is not asking this generation to remember for their own sakes. He is asking them to get something across two generational handovers, to people not yet born, who will never have seen any of it.

That is the hinge on which the survival of faith in a family turns, and it turns every generation. The exodus generation saw the sea. Their children saw the wilderness. Their grandchildren would see nothing but a settled country and hear only what they were told. The whole future of Israel’s knowledge of God depended on whether ordinary parents kept talking.

Read the stated purpose carefully too: that they may learn to fear me all the days that they live on the earth, and that they may teach their children so. The aim of the teaching is not information transfer. It is the fear of God — reverent awe — and the proof that it landed is that the next generation passes it on in turn.

verseByVerse.quote: And you came near and stood at the foot of the mountain, while the mountain burned with fire to the heart of heaven, wrapped in darkness, cloud, and gloom. Then the LORD spoke to you out of the midst of the fire. You heard the sound of words, but saw no form; there was only a voice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And you came near and stood at the foot of the mountain, while the mountain burned with fire to the heart of heaven, wrapped in darkness, cloud, and gloom. Then the LORD spoke to you out of the midst of the fire. You heard the sound of words, but saw no form; there was only a voice.

Here is the theological centre of the chapter and one of the most important sentences in the Old Testament, so read it slowly.

Everything about the scene is overwhelming to the eye. A mountain on fire to the height of heaven, and around the fire darkness, cloud and gloom — three words for the same thing, piled up. The most spectacular event in the religious history of the world, and the deliberate effect of the darkness is that there was nothing to look at.

And then: You heard the sound of words, but saw no form; there was only a voice.

God revealed himself by speaking. Not by appearing, not by manifesting a shape, not through a vision of something with edges — through words, which is the way one person makes himself known to another. That single fact is the ground of the second commandment, the reason Israel’s worship had no image at its centre when every other nation’s did, and the reason the Christian faith has always been carried by preaching rather than by spectacle. Faith comes from hearing (Rom. 10:17), and it comes that way because of what happened at Horeb.

But hold the sentence a moment longer, because the New Testament does something with it that nobody at Sinai could have anticipated. No one has ever seen God; the only God, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known (John 1:18) — and, four verses earlier, the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory (John 1:14).

At the mountain there was a voice and no form. In Bethlehem the voice took a form. The God who would not be represented by anything he had made represented himself, in a body, once — and men who had eaten fish with him wrote afterwards, that which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we looked upon and have touched with our hands (1 John 1:1).

verseByVerse.quote: And he declared to you his covenant, which he commanded you to perform, that is, the Ten Commandments, and he wrote them on two tablets of stone. And the LORD commanded me at that time to teach you statutes and rules, that you might do them in the land that you are going over to possess.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he declared to you his covenant, which he commanded you to perform, that is, the Ten Commandments, and he wrote them on two tablets of stone.

Two details here mark the Ten Commandments off from everything else in the law, and they are easy to miss.

First, God spoke them directly to the whole nation. Everything else in the Pentateuch came through Moses; these were heard by everybody, in the open air, from the fire, with no mediator in between. Second, God wrote them himself, on stone, with his own finger (Exod. 31:18) — while the rest of the law was written down by Moses on materials that would not last.

Nothing else in Scripture was delivered like that. Whatever else the Ten Commandments are, they are the part of God’s law that he took the trouble to say out loud to everybody and to carve in rock.

And verse 14 marks the distinction from the other side: And the LORD commanded me at that time to teach you statutes and rules. The Ten came from the fire; the rest came from Moses. Both are God’s word, and the manner of their giving is not identical, and the text is careful about it.

The word rendered covenant is the key one. These are not ten pieces of good advice or a moral system detached from a relationship. They are the terms of a bond between a God who had already rescued this people and a people who now belonged to him — which is exactly why the first thing the fire said was not a command at all, but a reminder: I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–24 — The Warning Against Idolatry: A Consuming Fire
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because they saw no form, Israel must make no idol of any kind; God is a jealous, consuming fire who will not share his glory, and idolatry will bring exile.
verseByVerse.theology: God is a consuming fire and a jealous God; idolatry is spiritual adultery that provokes his holy jealousy and brings judgment.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel was warned against carved images. Now: we guard against the subtler idols of the heart that rival God’s exclusive claim.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore watch yourselves very carefully. Since you saw no form on the day that the LORD spoke to you at Horeb out of the midst of the fire, beware lest you act corruptly by making a carved image for yourselves, in the form of any figure, the likeness of male or female, the likeness of any animal that is on the earth, the likeness of any winged bird that flies in the air, the likeness of anything that creeps on the ground, the likeness of any fish that is in the water under the earth. And beware lest you raise your eyes to heaven, and when you see the sun and the moon and the stars, all the host of heaven, you be drawn away and bow down to them and serve them, things that the LORD your God has allotted to all the peoples under the whole heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore watch yourselves very carefully. Since you saw no form on the day that the LORD spoke to you at Horeb out of the midst of the fire, beware lest you act corruptly by making a carved image for yourselves.

The argument is airtight and it hangs on one word: since. Because God showed no shape, to give him a shape is to say something false about him. That is what an idol is. Not primarily a rival to God — a lie about God, a statement in wood or stone that he is like this, when he never said he was.

Then the catalogue, and it runs in a very particular order: male or female… any animal that is on the earth… any winged bird that flies in the air… anything that creeps on the ground… any fish that is in the water. That is Genesis 1 played backwards — man, then beasts, then birds, then creeping things, then fish. Moses walks back down the ladder of creation, ruling out every rung, because every idol ever made is a piece of the creation promoted.

And then he raises his eyes: beware lest you raise your eyes to heaven, and when you see the sun and the moon and the stars, all the host of heaven, you be drawn away and bow down to them. Even the highest and cleanest things in the visible world — the ones that look most like gods, and which nearly every ancient civilisation worshipped — are on the wrong side of the line. They were made on the fourth day.

Verse 19 ends with a phrase readers stumble over: those are things that the LORD your God has allotted to all the peoples under the whole heaven. The most natural sense is that God gave the sun, moon and stars to all mankind — for light, for seasons, for everyone alike (Gen. 1:14). He did not give them as gods; he gave them as lamps, to everybody.

Now bring it home, because almost nobody reading this owns a carved image. The commandment is not really about statues. It is about the picture of God that a man carries in his head — one assembled out of his father, his temperament, his culture and his preferences, and then treated as though it were the real thing. That image is a carved image; it is simply carved somewhere you cannot see it. And the test is the same as it was at Horeb: has God said he is like that, or have you decided it?

verseByVerse.quote: But the LORD has taken you and brought you out of the iron furnace, out of Egypt, to be a people of his own inheritance, as you are this day. Furthermore, the LORD was angry with me because of you, and he swore that I should not cross the Jordan, and that I should not enter the good land that the LORD your God is giving you for an inheritance. For I must die in this land; I must not go over the Jordan. But you shall go over and take possession of that good land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the LORD has taken you and brought you out of the iron furnace, out of Egypt, to be a people of his own inheritance, as you are this day.

The iron furnace is a smelting furnace — the fierce, enclosed heat in which ore is melted so the metal can be separated out. It is a brutal image for four hundred years, and Scripture uses it deliberately: Egypt was not merely captivity, it was a fire.

Set that image beside the other fire in this chapter and you see what Moses is doing. There is the fire of Egypt, which was slavery. There is the fire on the mountain, which was revelation. There will be, in three verses, the fire that God himself is. The whole chapter is organised around fire, and God brought his people out of one and into the presence of another.

Then the phrase that ought to stop us: he brought them out to be a people of his own inheritance. An inheritance is what a man receives and keeps and hands on — the thing of lasting value that is properly his. Israel was God’s. Not his workforce, not his subjects — his portion. Paul prays that Christians would grasp exactly this, and it takes him a whole clause to say: the riches of his glorious inheritance in the saints (Eph. 1:18). The inheritance is us.

And then Moses mentions his own exclusion for the third time in four chapters (1:37; 3:26; 4:21). He cannot leave it alone. It is not self-pity — he says it every time in the middle of warning them about the consequences of sin, as the nearest and costliest illustration he has. His last sermon uses his own funeral as an argument.

verseByVerse.quote: Take care, lest you forget the covenant of the LORD your God, which he made with you, and make a carved image, the form of anything that the LORD your God has forbidden you. For the LORD your God is a consuming fire, a jealous God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take care, lest you forget the covenant of the LORD your God… For the LORD your God is a consuming fire, a jealous God.

Two words that modern readers flinch at, and both need explaining rather than softening.

A consuming fire. Not a warm hearth, not a symbol of enthusiasm. Fire is the thing in this chapter that spoke from the mountain, and it is the same fire that will not tolerate a rival in the camp. God’s holiness is not passive; it acts on what comes near it, and the same presence that gives light and warmth to those who belong to him will burn what is set up against him. The New Testament quotes this verse at Christians, not at pagans, and does not soften it a syllable: for our God is a consuming fire (Heb. 12:29).

A jealous God. English has almost lost the word, so hear it properly. Jealousy in Scripture is not envy — envy wants what belongs to somebody else, and God has no rival worth coveting. Jealousy is the rightful refusal of a husband to share his wife. It is the exact opposite of indifference. A man who watches his wife leave with somebody else and feels nothing does not love her; he has simply stopped caring what she does.

God had married this nation at that mountain. The covenant language of Deuteronomy is marriage language, and idolatry throughout the prophets is adultery, not merely error. So when Moses says God is jealous, he is not warning them about a divine temper. He is telling them how much they are loved, and what it will cost them to treat that love as though it did not matter.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses foresees that Israel will eventually fall into idolatry and be scattered among the nations, yet promises that if they seek the LORD with all their heart from exile, the merciful God will not forsake his covenant.
verseByVerse.theology: God’s judgment on idolatry is certain, but his covenant mercy is greater; he disciplines but will not abandon his people, for he is a merciful God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: exile and restoration were prophesied centuries in advance. Now: the believer who wanders can always return, for God meets the seeking heart with mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you father children and children's children, and have grown old in the land, and you act corruptly by making a carved image in the form of anything, and by doing what is evil in the sight of the LORD your God, so as to provoke him to anger, I call heaven and earth to witness against you today, that you will soon utterly perish from the land that you are going over the Jordan to possess. You will not live long in it, but will be utterly destroyed. And the LORD will scatter you among the peoples, and you will be left few in number among the nations where the LORD will drive you. And there you will serve gods of wood and stone, the work of human hands, that neither see, nor hear, nor eat, nor smell.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Moses does something extraordinary. He looks down the centuries and describes, in detail, exactly how this will go wrong.

When you father children and children’s children, and have grown old in the land, and you act corruptly by making a carved image… you will soon utterly perish from the land… And the LORD will scatter you among the peoples.

Notice the timing he gives it. Not the first generation, and not in a crisis. When you have grown old in the land — after the settling, after the vineyards are producing and the houses are built and nobody alive remembers a tent. Prosperity, not persecution, is what he expects to undo them. That is the pattern of the whole Bible and of most Christian lives; very few people are argued out of faith, and a great many are comfortable out of it.

I call heaven and earth to witness against you today. That is courtroom language. In the treaties of the ancient world, the gods of both parties were named as witnesses; Israel has no such gods to call, so Moses summons creation itself to the stand.

And then the sentence, and the shape of it is exact: there you will serve gods of wood and stone, the work of human hands, that neither see, nor hear, nor eat, nor smell.

The punishment fits the crime with terrible precision. You wanted a god you could see, so you will be given gods that cannot see you. You wanted one you could handle, so you will get ones that cannot handle anything. And the Psalms name what this does to a person over time: Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them (Ps. 115:8). Whatever a man worships, he grows to resemble. That is true of an idol of wood, and it is true of money, and it is true of Christ — which is the only reason any of us has any hope of becoming anything worth being.

verseByVerse.quote: But from there you will seek the LORD your God and you will find him, if you search after him with all your heart and with all your soul. When you are in tribulation, and all these things come upon you in the latter days, you will return to the LORD your God and obey his voice. For the LORD your God is a merciful God. He will not leave you or destroy you or forget the covenant with your fathers that he swore to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And then, out of the middle of the worst thing Moses has said yet, comes this.

But from there you will seek the LORD your God and you will find him, if you search after him with all your heart and with all your soul.

From there. Not from the land. Not after they have got themselves back. From exile — from the far country, from the middle of the consequences, from the place their own idolatry put them, surrounded by the wooden gods they chose. That is where the promise is addressed, and God puts the address in the sentence so that nobody can claim to be too far away for it.

Read what is required: not a sacrifice, not a pilgrimage, not restitution, not a temple — there will be no temple. Seek and search after him with all your heart. The whole heart, not a divided one; but nothing else, and nothing they could not do in Babylon.

And then verse 30 shifts from condition to prediction: you will return to the LORD your God and obey his voice. Not you may. Moses is not merely leaving a door open; he says they will come through it. The God who foresees the apostasy in verse 25 foresees the homecoming in verse 30, and he tells them so before either has happened.

Then the ground of the whole thing, and it is not in them: For the LORD your God is a merciful God. He will not leave you or destroy you or forget the covenant with your fathers that he swore to them.

The word for merciful is rachum, built on the word for a womb — the compassion a mother has for the child she carried, which is not a response to anything the child has done. And the security is an oath sworn to men centuries dead. Israel’s way home from exile did not depend on Israel’s performance in exile. It rested on a promise God made to Abraham before any of them existed, and on a mercy that is simply what he is like.

The Lord Jesus told this chapter as a story once. A son who took everything, went to a far country, spent it on idols and ended up feeding pigs — and when he came to himself, he went home, and his father saw him a long way off and ran (Luke 15:17–20). Deuteronomy 4:29 is where that road home was surveyed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–40 — There Is No Other: The Incomparable God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses calls Israel to consider that no other nation has ever heard God speak from fire or been redeemed by such mighty acts, all to prove the great confession: the LORD is God, and there is no other.
verseByVerse.theology: The LORD alone is God; his unique acts of revelation and redemption prove his exclusive deity and demand exclusive devotion.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel’s history was unrepeatable proof of the one true God. Now: the resurrection of Christ is God’s unanswerable proof that he alone is God and Savior.

verseByVerse.quote: "For ask now of the days that are past, which were before you, since the day that God created man on the earth, and ask from one end of heaven to the other, whether such a great thing as this has ever happened or was ever heard of. Did any people ever hear the voice of a god speaking out of the midst of the fire, as you have heard, and still live? Or has any god ever attempted to go and take a nation for himself from the midst of another nation, by trials, by signs, by wonders, and by war, by a mighty hand and an outstretched arm, and by great deeds of terror, all of which the LORD your God did for you in Egypt before your eyes?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For ask now of the days that are past, which were before you, since the day that God created man on the earth, and ask from one end of heaven to the other, whether such a great thing as this has ever happened or was ever heard of.

Moses issues a challenge with no limits on it. Search all of time — back to the creation of man. Search all of space — from one end of heaven to the other. Find a parallel.

Then the two questions. Did any people ever hear the voice of a god speaking out of the midst of the fire, as you have heard, and still live? And: has any god ever attempted to go and take a nation for himself from the midst of another nation, by trials, by signs, by wonders, and by war, by a mighty hand and an outstretched arm?

The second is the more staggering, and its force is lost on us because we no longer think as the ancient world did. Gods belonged to nations. A god of Egypt was for Egyptians; he had a territory, a people and a temple, and his fortunes rose and fell with theirs. The notion of a god crossing a border into the strongest empire on earth to extract a slave population — not a favoured people, a slave population, the lowest thing in that society — and make them his own, is not a variation on ancient religion. There is no category for it.

And notice the word attempted. Has any god even tried? Not merely succeeded — tried. The gods of the nations did not go and get anybody. They stayed where they were and waited to be fed.

That is the shape of the God of the Bible from beginning to end, and it does not change at the incarnation; it intensifies. He is not found at the top of a climb. He comes down into a foreign country and takes people out of it, at his own cost, and the whole of Christianity is a footnote to that habit of his.

verseByVerse.quote: To you it was shown, that you might know that the LORD is God; there is no other besides him. Out of heaven he let you hear his voice, that he might discipline you. And on earth he let you see his great fire, and you heard his words out of the midst of the fire. And because he loved your fathers and chose their offspring after them and brought you out of Egypt with his own presence, by his great power, driving out before you nations greater and mightier than you, to bring you in, to give you their land for an inheritance, as it is this day,
verseByVerse.commentary:
To you it was shown, that you might know that the LORD is God; there is no other besides him.

Here is the purpose of everything Moses has just listed. The plagues, the sea, the fire, the voice, the forty years — all of it had one aim, and it was not Israel’s comfort or even Israel’s freedom. It was that they should know something.

Every event in the exodus was a lesson. God was teaching a nation of slaves, over forty years, by means of an entire national history, one fact: that he is God and there is no other. The scale of the pedagogy tells you the difficulty of the lesson.

Verse 36 puts the two halves of that education side by side: Out of heaven he let you hear his voice, that he might discipline you. And on earth he let you see his great fire. The word behind discipline is yasar — to train, to instruct, the word for what a father does to a son he intends to make into something. It is not punishment. Sinai was a classroom with the roof off.

Then verse 37, and it answers the question the whole passage raises. Why them? Because he loved your fathers and chose their offspring after them and brought you out of Egypt with his own presence, by his great power.

There is the reason, and it is not a reason at all in the ordinary sense. He loved them. Not because they were numerous — they were not. Not because they were good — three chapters have just established the opposite. Deuteronomy will say it even more bluntly later: It was not because you were more in number than any other people that the LORD set his love on you… but it is because the LORD loves you (7:7–8). The love is its own explanation and there is nothing underneath it.

And note the means: with his own presence — the Hebrew says with his face. He did not send. He came.

verseByVerse.quote: know therefore today, and lay it to your heart, that the LORD is God in heaven above and on the earth beneath; there is no other. Therefore you shall keep his statutes and his commandments, which I command you today, that it may go well with you and with your children after you, and that you may prolong your days in the land that the LORD your God is giving you for all time."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Know therefore today, and lay it to your heart, that the LORD is God in heaven above and on the earth beneath; there is no other.

Two commands, and the second is the harder one.

Know — settle it as a fact. And then lay it to your heart, which is the Hebrew way of saying: bring it down out of your head and put it where your decisions are made. Moses evidently did not think the first would produce the second automatically, and he was right.

Every Christian knows the gap. A man can hold, without hesitation, that God is God in heaven above and on the earth beneath — and can still lie awake at three in the morning managing the universe on God’s behalf, or make a decision out of fear of somebody who will be dead in forty years. The doctrine is filed correctly and it is not running anything. Lay it to your heart is the work of a lifetime and it does not happen by learning more.

Notice also how comprehensive the claim is: in heaven above and on the earth beneath. Not the God of a nation or a territory or a sphere. There is no jurisdiction he does not hold, which is precisely what no other god of that world ever claimed, and precisely why an Israelite in exile — under Babylon’s gods, in Babylon’s land — could still pray.

And then, inevitably, verse 40: Therefore you shall keep his statutes and his commandments. The therefore is the whole logic of Deuteronomy. Obedience is not the foundation; it is the roof. First know who he is, then lay it to heart, and only then keep his commandments — because a command obeyed by someone who has not done the first two things is mere compliance, and it never lasts a generation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 41–43 — The Cities of Refuge East of the Jordan
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses sets apart three cities of refuge east of the Jordan, where one who kills unintentionally may flee and find safety from the avenger of blood.
verseByVerse.theology: God provides refuge for the guilty-but-not-malicious, foreshadowing Christ as the refuge to whom sinners flee for safety from judgment.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the manslayer fled to a city of refuge. Now: sinners flee to Christ, our refuge, who shelters us from the wrath we deserve.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses set apart three cities in the east beyond the Jordan, that the manslayer might flee there, anyone who kills his neighbor unintentionally, without being at enmity with him in time past; he may flee to one of these cities and save his life: Bezer in the wilderness on the tableland for the Reubenites, Ramoth in Gilead for the Gadites, and Golan in Bashan for the Manassites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now the strangest paragraph in the chapter. Moses has just finished the highest theology in the Pentateuch — the voice from the fire, there is no other God, know it and lay it to your heart — and the very next thing he does is a piece of administration.

Then Moses set apart three cities in the east beyond the Jordan, that the manslayer might flee there, anyone who kills his neighbour unintentionally, without being at enmity with him in time past. Bezer, Ramoth and Golan. Three towns, named, mapped, allocated.

Consider what he is doing. These cities are for a man who has not yet killed anybody, who may not yet be born, whose axe head will fly off a handle some afternoon decades from now in a country Moses will never enter. He is making arrangements for a stranger’s worst day, in a future he has been told he has no part in.

That is what the high theology of verses 32–40 is for. A man who genuinely believes there is no other God, in heaven above or on the earth beneath, will find himself doing small concrete kindnesses for people he will never meet. Doctrine that does not come down into three named towns on a map has not been laid to the heart yet.

And it is mercy, precisely. Not a reward for the innocent — a shelter for a man who has genuinely taken a life and will have to live with it. The chapter that establishes that God is a consuming fire ends by building somewhere for the guilty to run.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 44–49 — The Setting of the Law
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A summary heading introduces the great body of law that follows, locating it geographically and historically after the defeat of Sihon and Og.
verseByVerse.theology: God’s law is given in real history to a redeemed people; revelation is anchored in concrete time and place.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the law was set before Israel in the land of the defeated kings. Now: God’s Word comes to us as historical, located revelation, not abstract philosophy.

verseByVerse.quote: This is the law that Moses set before the people of Israel. These are the testimonies, the statutes, and the rules, which Moses spoke to the people of Israel when they came out of Egypt, beyond the Jordan in the valley opposite Beth-peor, in the land of Sihon the king of the Amorites, who lived at Heshbon, whom Moses and the people of Israel defeated when they came out of Egypt. And they took possession of his land and the land of Og, the king of Bashan, the two kings of the Amorites, who lived to the east beyond the Jordan; from Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, as far as Mount Sirion (that is, Hermon), together with all the Arabah on the east side of the Jordan as far as the Sea of the Arabah, under the slopes of Pisgah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the law that Moses set before the people of Israel. These are the testimonies, the statutes, and the rules, which Moses spoke to the people of Israel when they came out of Egypt.

A heading, and a hinge. The first address is over; from chapter 5 the great body of the law begins, and this paragraph is the title page.

Three words are used for what follows and they are not synonyms piled up for effect. Testimonies are what God has borne witness to about himself. Statutes are things engraved, fixed, not up for revision. Rules are judgments — the decisions of a judge, applied to cases. Together they cover what God has declared, what he has fixed, and how it works out in the ordinary disputes of life.

Then the location, given at length: beyond the Jordan in the valley opposite Beth-peor, in the land of Sihon the king of the Amorites… whom Moses and the people of Israel defeated when they came out of Egypt.

Every element of that address is a sermon. Beyond the Jordan — outside the land, still on the wrong bank. Opposite Beth-peor — facing the scene of the nation’s most recent and most shameful collapse. In the land of Sihon… whom they defeated — standing on ground God had already given them.

So the law of God is delivered to a people who are camped between their worst failure and their unclaimed inheritance, on a piece of land that proves he keeps his promises. That is not a bad description of where the church stands whenever Scripture is opened: our failures behind us and in plain view, the promise ahead of us and not yet possessed, and enough already given to make it unreasonable to doubt the rest.

4.theology:
The God who reveals himself by his Word. At Horeb, Israel “heard the sound of words, but saw no form” (4:12). God comes by speaking, not by appearing in shape; this grounds the prohibition of images and the priority of hearing in all true worship. The speaking God is fully revealed in the Word made flesh (John 1; Heb 1:1–2).

A consuming fire, a jealous God. God’s holiness is a blazing fire (4:24; Heb 12:29), and his jealousy is the righteous ardor of a husband who will not share his bride. Yet this same fire fell on Christ at Calvary, so that the redeemed are embraced rather than consumed.

There is no other. The whole sermon aims at one confession: “the LORD is God; there is no other besides him” (4:35, 39). His unrepeatable acts in history prove his exclusive deity, supremely now in the resurrection of Christ, and demand exclusive, heartfelt devotion.
4.examples:
Then: Israel stood as the most privileged nation on earth — a people who heard God’s voice from the fire, were redeemed from the iron furnace, and received righteous laws that would make the nations marvel — and Moses pleaded with them to remember, to shun idols, and to know that the LORD alone is God.

Now: We who have a God nearer than our breath, who hears us “whenever we call,” must still guard our hearts against the idol-factory within, teach the mighty acts of God to our children, and flee for refuge to Christ from the wrath we deserve. The consuming fire is our Father; the jealous God is our faithful husband; and the merciful God meets every seeking heart, however far it has wandered, with the welcome of grace.

5.title: The Ten Commandments Repeated: Grace Before Law
5.text: <sup>1</sup>And Moses summoned all Israel and said to them, "Hear, O Israel, the statutes and the rules that I speak in your hearing today, and you shall learn them and be careful to do them.<sup>2</sup>The LORD our God made a covenant with us in Horeb.<sup>3</sup>Not with our fathers did the LORD make this covenant, but with us, who are all of us here alive today.<sup>4</sup>The LORD spoke with you face to face at the mountain, out of the midst of the fire,<sup>5</sup>while I stood between the LORD and you at that time, to declare to you the word of the LORD. For you were afraid because of the fire, and you did not go up into the mountain. He said:<sup>6</sup>"'I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.<sup>7</sup>"'You shall have no other gods before me.<sup>8</sup>"'You shall not make for yourself a carved image, or any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or that is on the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth.<sup>9</sup>You shall not bow down to them or serve them, for I the LORD your God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me,<sup>10</sup>but showing steadfast love to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments.<sup>11</sup>"'You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain, for the LORD will not hold him guiltless who takes his name in vain.<sup>12</sup>"'Observe the Sabbath day, to keep it holy, as the LORD your God commanded you.<sup>13</sup>Six days you shall labor and do all your work,<sup>14</sup>but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God. On it you shall not do any work, you or your son or your daughter or your male servant or your female servant, or your ox or your donkey or any of your livestock, or the sojourner who is within your gates, that your male servant and your female servant may rest as well as you.<sup>15</sup>You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God brought you out from there with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm. Therefore the LORD your God commanded you to keep the Sabbath day.<sup>16</sup>"'Honor your father and your mother, as the LORD your God commanded you, that your days may be long, and that it may go well with you in the land that the LORD your God is giving you.<sup>17</sup>"'You shall not murder.<sup>18</sup>"'And you shall not commit adultery.<sup>19</sup>"'And you shall not steal.<sup>20</sup>"'And you shall not bear false witness against your neighbor.<sup>21</sup>"'And you shall not covet your neighbor's wife. And you shall not desire your neighbor's house, his field, or his male servant, or his female servant, his ox, or his donkey, or anything that is your neighbor's.'<sup>22</sup>"These words the LORD spoke to all your assembly at the mountain out of the midst of the fire, the cloud, and the thick darkness, with a loud voice; and he added no more. And he wrote them on two tablets of stone and gave them to me.<sup>23</sup>And as soon as you heard the voice out of the midst of the darkness, while the mountain was burning with fire, you came near to me, all the heads of your tribes, and your elders.<sup>24</sup>And you said, 'Behold, the LORD our God has shown us his glory and greatness, and we have heard his voice out of the midst of the fire. This day we have seen God speak with man, and man still live.<sup>25</sup>Now therefore why should we die? For this great fire will consume us. If we hear the voice of the LORD our God any more, we shall die.<sup>26</sup>For who is there of all flesh, that has heard the voice of the living God speaking out of the midst of fire as we have, and has still lived?<sup>27</sup>Go near and hear all that the LORD our God will say, and speak to us all that the LORD our God will speak to you, and we will hear and do it.'<sup>28</sup>"And the LORD heard your words, when you spoke to me. And the LORD said to me, 'I have heard the words of this people, which they have spoken to you. They are right in all that they have spoken.<sup>29</sup>Oh that they had such a heart as this always, to fear me and to keep all my commandments, that it might go well with them and with their descendants forever!<sup>30</sup>Go and say to them, "Return to your tents."<sup>31</sup>But you, stand here by me, and I will tell you the whole commandment and the statutes and the rules that you shall teach them, that they may do them in the land that I am giving them to possess.'<sup>32</sup>You shall be careful therefore to do as the LORD your God has commanded you. You shall not turn aside to the right hand or to the left.<sup>33</sup>You shall walk in all the way that the LORD your God has commanded you, that you may live, and that it may go well with you, and that you may live long in the land that you shall possess.
5.overview:
Chapter 5 opens the great body of covenant law by returning to its foundation: the Ten Commandments, the very words God spoke from the fire at Horeb. Moses repeats the Decalogue to a new generation, insisting with passionate immediacy that the covenant is theirs — “not with our fathers… but with us, who are all of us here alive today” (5:3). The covenant is never a museum-piece; it is living and present for every generation that hears.

The prologue to the commandments is pure gospel: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery” (5:6). Before a single command is given, grace is announced. God redeems first, then commands. The law is the response of a freed people, never the price of their freedom.

A striking difference appears in the Sabbath commandment: where Exodus grounds it in creation, Deuteronomy grounds it in redemption — “you shall remember that you were a slave in Egypt” (5:15). The rest of the redeemed is rooted in the rest God has given.

The chapter closes with the people’s terror at God’s voice and their plea for Moses to mediate, and with God’s aching wish: “Oh that they had such a heart as this always, to fear me and to keep all my commandments” (5:29). The law is holy and good, but Israel needs a new heart — a longing the gospel alone fulfills.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The Covenant Is Ours Today
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses summons Israel to hear the statutes, insisting the Horeb covenant was made not merely with their fathers but with them, the living generation, who heard God face to face.
verseByVerse.theology: The covenant is ever-present and personal; each generation must own it as made with them, not relegate it to history.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the new generation claimed Horeb as their own covenant. Now: every believer must personally embrace the gospel, not inherit it secondhand.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses summoned all Israel and said to them, "Hear, O Israel, the statutes and the rules that I speak in your hearing today, and you shall learn them and be careful to do them. The LORD our God made a covenant with us in Horeb. Not with our fathers did the LORD make this covenant, but with us, who are all of us here alive today.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear, O Israel, the statutes and the rules that I speak in your hearing today.

Hear, O Israel — shema Yisrael. The phrase begins here and will reach its summit in the next chapter, and it sets the posture of the whole book. Before Israel does anything, she listens.

Then Moses says something that ought to stop the reader: The LORD our God made a covenant with us in Horeb. Not with our fathers did the LORD make this covenant, but with us, who are all of us here alive today.

On the face of it that is not accurate. The covenant at Horeb was made with their fathers — and their fathers are dead in the wilderness, every one of them but two. The men listening were children then, or not yet born.

Moses knows that perfectly well; he has just spent three chapters on those graves. He is making a preaching point, and it is one of the most important in Scripture. The covenant is not a historical artefact that happened to somebody else and was handed down like a title deed. It binds the living. Every generation stands at Sinai for itself.

Which puts a question to anybody raised inside the faith. It is entirely possible to be the third generation in a Christian family, to know the language, hold the doctrines, keep the habits, and never once to have transacted anything with God personally. That is a covenant made with our fathers. Moses will not permit it. Not with our fathers… but with us, who are all of us here alive today — and today is the great word of this book, appearing in it more than fifty times.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke with you face to face at the mountain, out of the midst of the fire, while I stood between the LORD and you at that time, to declare to you the word of the LORD. For you were afraid because of the fire, and you did not go up into the mountain. He said:
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD spoke with you face to face at the mountain, out of the midst of the fire, while I stood between the LORD and you at that time, to declare to you the word of the LORD. For you were afraid because of the fire, and you did not go up into the mountain.

Two things are said in one breath and they pull against each other. God spoke face to face — the phrase for direct, unmediated, personal address, the way a man speaks to a friend. And Moses stood between.

Both are true, and the tension is the entire situation of fallen man before God. He came near enough to be heard by everybody, in the open, without a priest or a ritual or a temple. And they could not bear it. The nearness they had been given was more than they could survive, so a man stood in the gap and carried the words across.

Keep that picture, because it does not go away. The whole of the Old Testament is arranged around men standing in the middle — Moses at the mountain, Aaron with a censer in a plague, the high priest behind the curtain once a year. Every one of them was temporary and every one of them died.

And when the New Testament states the matter, it uses this exact vocabulary and adds one word: For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2:5). One. Not a succession. The man who stood between the fire and the people at Horeb was doing, for a day, what Someone else would do permanently — and unlike Moses, he did not merely carry the words. He was them.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before any command is given, God announces redemption: he is the LORD who brought Israel out of slavery. Grace precedes law.
verseByVerse.theology: Redemption is the foundation of obedience; God saves first and commands second. The law is the response of a freed people, not the price of freedom.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel was freed before being commanded. Now: we obey out of gratitude for grace already received in Christ, never to earn salvation.

verseByVerse.quote: "'I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.
