Before a single you shall, this. It is the most important structural fact about the Ten Commandments and it is missed almost every time they are quoted.

Try the experiment. Read the Ten Commandments to somebody who has never heard them, and begin at verse 7. What you have given them is a moral code — a list of requirements, and they will naturally assume that keeping it is how you get in with God. Now read it again from verse 6. Everything changes. The commandments are not entrance conditions. They are the way a people already rescued now live.

God does not say keep these and I will bring you out of Egypt. They are already out. The sea is behind them; the chains are off; they have been carried through a desert for forty years. He identifies himself as the one who did that, and only then tells them how to live.

This is the shape of the whole Bible. Indicative before imperative; what God has done before what we must do; Romans 1–11 before Romans 12. And it is the difference between religion and the gospel, which is not a difference in the commandments at all — the standards are identical — but a difference in what they are for. For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace (Rom. 6:14).

And note the last phrase: out of the house of slavery. Every one of the ten that follows is addressed to ex-slaves, by the God who unlocked the door. They are not a new set of chains from a new master. They are the description of what free people look like, written by the one who paid to make them free.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–15 — The First Table: Loving God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first commandments govern Israel’s relationship to God: no other gods, no idols, no misuse of his name, and the keeping of the Sabbath, grounded here in redemption.
verseByVerse.theology: The first table guards God’s exclusive worship, his proper representation, the honor of his name, and the rhythm of rest rooted in redemption.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel ordered worship around the one true God. Now: we keep God supreme, refuse idols of the heart, honor his name, and find rest in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "'You shall have no other gods before me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You shall have no other gods before me.

The Hebrew behind before me is literally before my face, or in my presence. That is stronger than it sounds in English, where before can suggest mere ranking — as though the commandment were about keeping God at the top of a list with other gods permitted underneath.

It is not about ranking. It is about location, and the location is everywhere. There is nowhere that is not in God’s presence, so there is nowhere a rival may be kept. A man may not have other gods in the back of the house.

And notice the form of the sentence. It does not say there are no other gods, although Deuteronomy will say that plainly enough (4:35, 39). It says you shall have no other gods — the issue is possession, allegiance, what you actually reckon with. A man’s real god is not the one he would name if asked. It is the one he consults when frightened, obeys when the two conflict, and cannot imagine living without.

That is a test anybody can run and few enjoy. Take the thing whose loss would make life feel not worth living, and you have found what is standing before his face.

verseByVerse.quote: "'You shall not make for yourself a carved image, or any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or that is on the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth. You shall not bow down to them or serve them, for I the LORD your God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, but showing steadfast love to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second commandment governs not whom Israel worships but how. A man may be aiming at the true God and still be worshipping falsely, if he has made himself an image and put it in the way.

Then the sanction, and it troubles people: visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children to the third and the fourth generation of those who hate me, but showing steadfast love to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments.

Three things make this clear. First, read the qualifier: of those who hate me. The children in view are not innocent parties punished for an ancestor’s sin; they are children who have taken up their fathers’ hatred and continued in it. Scripture is emphatic elsewhere that this is not arbitrary — the son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father (Ezek. 18:20).

Second, what is described is largely observable. Sin runs in families. Everybody has seen a household where the same thing has gone round three times — the drinking, the temper, the absence, the coldness — each generation learning it from the one before and calling it normal. God is not inventing that mechanism here; he is naming it.

Third, and this is the point most often missed, look at the arithmetic. Three or four generations of consequence set against thousands — the Hebrew can be read as thousands of generations. The two halves of the verse are not balanced and are not meant to be. God is telling a people about to be given a law that his mercy outweighs his judgment by a margin no one can count.

Which is exactly how he describes himself when Moses asks to see his glory: The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness, keeping steadfast love for thousands (Exod. 34:6–7).

verseByVerse.quote: "'You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain, for the LORD will not hold him guiltless who takes his name in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain, for the LORD will not hold him guiltless who takes his name in vain.

The verb is lift up or carry, and in vain means emptily, to no purpose, for nothing. So the commandment forbids picking up the name of God and carrying it around empty.

Profanity is the least of it. A man who curses using the name of God at least believes it has weight; that is why he reaches for it. The commandment goes far wider.

It covers the false oath — swearing by God’s name to something untrue, which is to make God the guarantor of a lie. It covers the prayer that uses his name as a formula. And most searchingly, it covers claiming God’s authority for what he has not said: attaching his name to our own preferences, our politics, our certainty about somebody else’s motives, and telling people that God is behind it. That is carrying his name emptily, and it is done most often by people who would never swear.

And there is a further layer for anybody who bears his name. Israel had the name of God put upon her (Num. 6:27); Christians are called by the name of Christ. To wear that name and live emptily — to be identifiably his and no different — is a way of taking the name in vain that requires no words at all.

The warning attached is unusually severe: the LORD will not hold him guiltless. This is the only one of the ten with that clause. God will not treat the misuse of his name as a small matter, and the reason is that his name is the revelation of who he is. To handle it carelessly is to handle him carelessly.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Observe the Sabbath day, to keep it holy, as the LORD your God commanded you. Six days you shall labor and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God. On it you shall not do any work, you or your son or your daughter or your male servant or your female servant, or your ox or your donkey or any of your livestock, or the sojourner who is within your gates, that your male servant and your female servant may rest as well as you. You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God brought you out from there with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm. Therefore the LORD your God commanded you to keep the Sabbath day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the great difference between this Decalogue and the one in Exodus 20, and it is not a discrepancy — it is a deliberate second lesson.

In Exodus, the Sabbath is grounded in creation: for in six days the LORD made heaven and earth… and rested on the seventh day (Exod. 20:11). Here it is grounded in redemption: You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God brought you out from there with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm. Therefore the LORD your God commanded you to keep the Sabbath day.

Both are true and they teach different things. Creation says rest is woven into the structure of the world; it is how the week was built, and a man who never stops is fighting the grain of the universe. Redemption says rest is what freedom looks like. In Egypt they worked and worked and there was no seventh day, because slaves do not get one. The Sabbath is a weekly re-enactment of the exodus: once a week Israel stopped, and every time she stopped she said out loud, with her body, I am not a slave any more.

And then look at the list of who rests, because Deuteronomy adds something Exodus does not. Son, daughter, male servant, female servant, ox, donkey, all your livestock, the sojourner within your gates — that your male servant and your female servant may rest as well as you.

There it is. The servants’ rest is given as the purpose. A man who had been a slave in Egypt is forbidden to turn his own household into what he came out of. The commandment reaches down past the head of the family to the foreign labourer and the working animals; in an agricultural economy, giving the ox a day off every week is a real and calculable cost, and God requires it.

The Lord Jesus stood in this tradition exactly when he said The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath (Mark 2:27) — and he is what it was always pointing at. So then, there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God, for whoever has entered God’s rest has also rested from his works as God did from his (Heb. 4:9–10). The weekly stop was a rehearsal. The rest itself is a Person, and entering it means giving up the exhausting business of justifying yourself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–21 — The Second Table: Loving Neighbor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The remaining commandments govern relationships among people: honoring parents, and prohibitions of murder, adultery, theft, false witness, and covetousness.
verseByVerse.theology: Love for God overflows into love for neighbor; the second table protects life, marriage, property, truth, and the contentment of the heart.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel’s society was ordered by these commands. Now: the same commands, deepened by Christ, govern the heart and the community of faith.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Honor your father and your mother, as the LORD your God commanded you, that your days may be long, and that it may go well with you in the land that the LORD your God is giving you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Honor your father and your mother, as the LORD your God commanded you, that your days may be long, and that it may go well with you in the land that the LORD your God is giving you.

This commandment stands at the hinge of the two tables, and its position is not accidental. Everything before it concerns God directly; everything after it concerns neighbours. Parents sit between, because they are the first authority any human being ever meets, and a child learns either submission or defiance long before he has any thoughts about God at all.

Honor is a heavy word — kabed, from the root meaning weight. To honour is to treat as weighty, to give somebody the significance they are due. It is not the same as agreement, and it is not the same as affection, which cannot be commanded. It is a settled way of treating a person.

Which matters, because this commandment is a hard one for a great many people. Not everybody had parents who were honourable. Scripture does not pretend otherwise, and it does not say obey your father and mother in everything — the same law elsewhere puts limits on what any human authority may require. But it does insist that a father and mother are to be treated as weighty, whatever else is true, and it is possible to do that for a parent who failed badly.

Note also that Deuteronomy adds a clause Exodus does not have: and that it may go well with you. Paul picks up both halves and observes something about them that is easy to walk past: “Honor your father and mother” (this is the first commandment with a promise), “that it may go well with you and that you may live long in the land” (Eph. 6:2–3). Of all ten, this is the one God chose to attach a reward to.

verseByVerse.quote: "'You shall not murder. "'And you shall not commit adultery. "'And you shall not steal. "'And you shall not bear false witness against your neighbor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four commandments in four short lines, and they cover the four things a neighbour cannot live without: his life, his marriage, his property, and his good name.

You shall not murder. The verb is ratsach, which is not the general word for killing; it does not touch warfare or judicial execution, both of which the same law regulates. It means the unlawful taking of a life, and the ground of the prohibition is given back in Genesis: for God made man in his own image (Gen. 9:6). What makes murder monstrous is not that human beings are useful but that they are stamped.

And you shall not commit adultery. Marriage is placed immediately after life, which is its own statement about how seriously God treats it.

And you shall not steal. Which assumes that property is real and that a man may rightly own things — an assumption the commandment is meaningless without.

And you shall not bear false witness against your neighbor. The setting is a courtroom. A society where testimony cannot be trusted has no way of protecting anybody, and the weak are the first to suffer.

Now, all four can be kept by a thoroughly bad man. That is precisely what the Lord Jesus said about them, and he did not soften the law but drove it inward: You have heard that it was said… “You shall not murder”… But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment (Matt. 5:21–22), and the same for adultery and the look that precedes it. He was not adding to Moses. He was refusing to let the commandments be reduced to a list of things a man has not done.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And you shall not covet your neighbor's wife. And you shall not desire your neighbor's house, his field, or his male servant, or his female servant, his ox, or his donkey, or anything that is your neighbor's.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And you shall not covet your neighbor’s wife. And you shall not desire your neighbor’s house, his field, or his male servant, or his female servant, his ox, or his donkey, or anything that is your neighbor’s.

The tenth is unlike the other nine, and the difference is the reason it is last.

Every other commandment can be broken visibly. Murder leaves a body, theft leaves a gap, adultery and false witness can be testified to. A man could keep the first nine outwardly for sixty years with a heart like a sewer, and no court on earth could touch him. The tenth reaches in and takes hold of what nobody can see, and it is the one that makes the other nine unkeepable.

Note that Deuteronomy puts the wife first, where Exodus 20:17 begins with the house — and it uses a different verb for her than for the property. She is not listed among a man’s goods here; she is set apart from them.

And this is the commandment that took Paul apart. He had kept the visible law impeccably and counted himself blameless — and then: I would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, “You shall not covet” (Rom. 7:7). The tenth commandment was the one that got in behind his defences, because it does not ask what he did.

Which is exactly what the law is for. It was never a ladder. It is a mirror, and the tenth commandment is the part of the glass that shows you your face rather than your hands. For by works of the law no human being will be justified in his sight, since through the law comes knowledge of sin (Rom. 3:20).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–33 — The People’s Fear and God’s Longing
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Terrified by God’s voice from the fire, the people beg Moses to mediate; God approves their fear and utters his aching wish that they had a heart to fear and obey him always.
verseByVerse.theology: Sinners cannot bear the unmediated presence of a holy God and need a mediator; the law reveals the need for a new heart that only grace can give.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel needed Moses to stand between them and God. Now: we draw near through Christ, our greater Mediator, and receive the new heart the law could not give.

verseByVerse.quote: "These words the LORD spoke to all your assembly at the mountain out of the midst of the fire, the cloud, and the thick darkness, with a loud voice; and he added no more. And he wrote them on two tablets of stone and gave them to me. And as soon as you heard the voice out of the midst of the darkness, while the mountain was burning with fire, you came near to me, all the heads of your tribes, and your elders. And you said, 'Behold, the LORD our God has shown us his glory and greatness, and we have heard his voice out of the midst of the fire. This day we have seen God speak with man, and man still live.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These words the LORD spoke to all your assembly at the mountain out of the midst of the fire, the cloud, and the thick darkness, with a loud voice; and he added no more.

And he added no more. God said these ten and stopped.

Everything else in the law — hundreds of statutes, the whole sacrificial system, the entire civil code — came through Moses. These ten God spoke himself, aloud, to the entire nation standing in the open, and then fell silent and wrote them down with his own hand on stone.

That is why the Ten Commandments have always occupied the place they do. It is not that the rest of Scripture is less inspired. It is that these are the words God chose to say out loud to everybody and to carve in rock, and the manner of their delivery is part of their meaning.

Then the people’s reaction, and it is not what a modern reader expects. Behold, the LORD our God has shown us his glory and greatness, and we have heard his voice out of the midst of the fire. This day we have seen God speak with man, and man still live.

Their astonishment is not that God spoke. It is that they were still standing afterwards. They had assumed — correctly — that hearing the voice of God would kill them, and they had just survived it, and they could not get over it. That is a category we have almost entirely lost. Our difficulty with God is that we cannot hear him; theirs was that they had, and were somehow not dead.

verseByVerse.quote: Now therefore why should we die? For this great fire will consume us. If we hear the voice of the LORD our God any more, we shall die. For who is there of all flesh, that has heard the voice of the living God speaking out of the midst of fire as we have, and has still lived? Go near and hear all that the LORD our God will say, and speak to us all that the LORD our God will speak to you, and we will hear and do it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And then the terror catches up with them. Now therefore why should we die? For this great fire will consume us. If we hear the voice of the LORD our God any more, we shall die. For who is there of all flesh, that has heard the voice of the living God speaking out of the midst of fire as we have, and has still lived?

This is not superstition and it is not cowardice. It is an accurate reading of their situation. Sinful people cannot stand in the unmediated presence of a holy God, and they had just worked that out for themselves, and they were right.

So they ask for a go-between: Go near and hear all that the LORD our God will say, and speak to us all that the LORD our God will speak to you, and we will hear and do it.

Read what they are actually requesting. Not less of God — they are not asking him to go away or to lower his standards. They are asking for a man who can survive the fire to bring them what is said in it. That is the most spiritually intelligent thing this nation ever says.

And it is the request every human being has, once they have understood the problem. The whole machinery of religion is people trying to solve it: priests, rituals, intermediaries, techniques for approaching a holy God without being destroyed. Israel at least asked God for the solution instead of inventing one, and the next verses record what he thought of that.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the LORD heard your words, when you spoke to me. And the LORD said to me, 'I have heard the words of this people, which they have spoken to you. They are right in all that they have spoken. Oh that they had such a heart as this always, to fear me and to keep all my commandments, that it might go well with them and with their descendants forever!
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the LORD heard your words when you spoke to me. And the LORD said to me, “I have heard the words of this people, which they have spoken to you. They are right in all that they have spoken.”

God endorses their fear. Not they should be braver, not they have misunderstood me — they are right. Their assessment of what it would cost them to hear his voice unmediated was correct, and he says so.

And then comes verse 29, which is one of the most extraordinary sentences God ever speaks.

Oh that they had such a heart as this always, to fear me and to keep all my commandments, that it might go well with them and with their descendants forever!

That is longing. The Hebrew is an exclamation of wish — literally who will give that they had such a heart. The God who needs nothing, who is complete in himself, who has just spoken the universe’s moral law out of a burning mountain, says: if only.

We should be careful here, and also honest. This is not a defect in God’s knowledge, as though he did not see what was coming; three verses of this book have already predicted the exile. It is a revelation of his disposition. He genuinely delights in the obedience of his people and genuinely grieves at its absence, and he wants us to know it. Ezekiel says the same thing in the same register: I have no pleasure in the death of anyone (Ezek. 18:32).

And notice what he wishes for. Not better behaviour — such a heart. He knows exactly where the problem is, and it is not in the commandments and not in the mediator. It is in them.

Now read on twenty-five chapters, and find the answer to God’s own wish: And the LORD your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring, so that you will love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul, that you may live (30:6). He says oh that they had such a heart — and then promises to give them one. That is the whole gospel in the space of one book: God asks for what we cannot produce, and then produces it in us himself. I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you (Ezek. 36:26).

verseByVerse.quote: Go and say to them, "Return to your tents." But you, stand here by me, and I will tell you the whole commandment and the statutes and the rules that you shall teach them, that they may do them in the land that I am giving them to possess.' You shall be careful therefore to do as the LORD your God has commanded you. You shall not turn aside to the right hand or to the left. You shall walk in all the way that the LORD your God has commanded you, that you may live, and that it may go well with you, and that you may live long in the land that you shall possess.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Go and say to them, “Return to your tents.” But you, stand here by me, and I will tell you the whole commandment.

Two destinations in one sentence, and the contrast is the shape of the chapter. The people go home. The mediator stays with God.

Picture the evening. Two million people walk back down the slope to their families, to the cooking fires and the children and the ordinary business of a camp — and one man is left standing on a burning mountain in the dark, being given the rest of the law. He does not go back to his tent. Somebody has to remain in the fire so that everybody else can go home, and that is what a mediator is for.

There is only one place in Scripture where that pattern is broken, and it is broken by the one who said Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matt. 11:28). He stood in the fire so that we could go home — and then, unlike Moses, he brought us with him.

The chapter ends with the charge: You shall be careful therefore to do as the LORD your God has commanded you. You shall not turn aside to the right hand or to the left. You shall walk in all the way that the LORD your God has commanded you, that you may live, and that it may go well with you.

Neither to the right nor to the left. There are two ways off a road and both of them are off it. A man can leave the way of God by laxity or by an excess of scruple, by loosening what God tied or by tying what God left free, and Deuteronomy is as worried about the second as the first — which is why the book opened by forbidding addition as well as subtraction (4:2). The road runs straight. Walk on it.

5.theology:
Grace before law. Before a single command, God declares, “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (5:6). Redemption is the foundation of obedience; the law is the grateful response of a freed people, never the price of their freedom. This gospel order governs all of Scripture and finds its fullness in the greater exodus of the cross.

The Sabbath rooted in redemption. Uniquely, Deuteronomy grounds the Sabbath not in creation but in deliverance: “you shall remember that you were a slave” (5:15). The rest of the redeemed points to the ultimate rest secured by Christ (Heb 4), into which we enter by faith.

The longing for a new heart. God’s aching wish — “Oh that they had such a heart as this always” (5:29) — exposes the central problem: the law commands a heart it cannot create. What God here longs for, he himself supplies in the new covenant, writing his law on hearts of flesh by the Spirit (Jer 31:33; Ezek 36:26).
5.examples:
Then: A new generation stood to claim the Horeb covenant as their own, hearing the Ten Words anew, trembling at God’s voice from the fire, and begging Moses to stand between them and the holy God — while God Himself longed for them to have a heart to obey him always.

Now: We must own the covenant of grace personally, not by inheritance; obey out of gratitude for the redemption already accomplished in Christ; honor God, neighbor, and the rhythm of rest he gives; and draw near through Jesus, our greater Mediator, who not only relays God’s word but removes our sin and gives the new heart the law could only long for.

6.title: The Shema and the Great Commandment: Love the LORD with All Your Heart
6.text: <sup>1</sup>"Now this is the commandment—the statutes and the rules —that the LORD your God commanded me to teach you, that you may do them in the land to which you are going over, to possess it,<sup>2</sup>that you may fear the LORD your God, you and your son and your son's son, by keeping all his statutes and his commandments, which I command you, all the days of your life, and that your days may be long.<sup>3</sup>Hear therefore, O Israel, and be careful to do them, that it may go well with you, and that you may multiply greatly, as the LORD, the God of your fathers, has promised you, in a land flowing with milk and honey.<sup>4</sup>"Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one.<sup>5</sup>You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might.<sup>6</sup>And these words that I command you today shall be on your heart.<sup>7</sup>You shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise.<sup>8</sup>You shall bind them as a sign on your hand, and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes.<sup>9</sup>You shall write them on the doorposts of your house and on your gates.<sup>10</sup>"And when the LORD your God brings you into the land that he swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, to give you—with great and good cities that you did not build,<sup>11</sup>and houses full of all good things that you did not fill, and cisterns that you did not dig, and vineyards and olive trees that you did not plant—and when you eat and are full,<sup>12</sup>then take care lest you forget the LORD, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.<sup>13</sup>It is the LORD your God you shall fear. Him you shall serve and by his name you shall swear.<sup>14</sup>You shall not go after other gods, the gods of the peoples who are around you—<sup>15</sup>for the LORD your God in your midst is a jealous God— lest the anger of the LORD your God be kindled against you, and he destroy you from off the face of the earth.<sup>16</sup>"You shall not put the LORD your God to the test, as you tested him at Massah.<sup>17</sup>You shall diligently keep the commandments of the LORD your God, and his testimonies and his statutes, which he has commanded you.<sup>18</sup>And you shall do what is right and good in the sight of the LORD, that it may go well with you, and that you may go in and take possession of the good land that the LORD swore to give to your fathers<sup>19</sup>by thrusting out all your enemies from before you, as the LORD has promised.<sup>20</sup>"When your son asks you in time to come, 'What is the meaning of the testimonies and the statutes and the rules that the LORD our God has commanded you?'<sup>21</sup>then you shall say to your son, 'We were Pharaoh's slaves in Egypt. And the LORD brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand.<sup>22</sup>And the LORD showed signs and wonders, great and grievous, against Egypt and against Pharaoh and all his household, before our eyes.<sup>23</sup>And he brought us out from there, that he might bring us in and give us the land that he swore to give to our fathers.<sup>24</sup>And the LORD commanded us to do all these statutes, to fear the LORD our God, for our good always, that he might preserve us alive, as we are this day.<sup>25</sup>And it will be righteousness for us, if we are careful to do all this commandment before the LORD our God, as he has commanded us.'
6.overview:
Chapter 6 contains what is arguably the single most important passage in the Old Testament — the Shema (from the Hebrew “Hear”): “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one. You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might” (6:4–5). For three thousand years devout Jews have recited these words morning and evening. And when Jesus was asked for the greatest commandment, he reached for this very verse (Mark 12:29–30). It is the heartbeat of all true religion.

Notice what the Shema commands: not merely obedience, ritual, or correct doctrine, but love — total, undivided, whole-souled love for the one true God. Religion that is not love is not what God asks. And this love is to saturate every sphere of life: heart, soul, and might.

Moses then gives the great method of passing faith on: these words are to be on the heart, taught diligently to children, talked of at home and on the road, bound on the hand and forehead, written on the doorposts. Faith is to permeate the ordinary fabric of daily life.

The chapter warns against the dangers of prosperity — that when Israel grows comfortable in the land, they will forget the God who gave it — and ends with the call to remember redemption and to tell the next generation the story of God’s saving acts. To love this God, and to hand that love on, is the whole vocation of God’s people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — The Purpose of the Law: Life and Multiplication
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses introduces the commandments as the path to life, long days, and flourishing in the land flowing with milk and honey, to be feared and obeyed across the generations.
verseByVerse.theology: Obedience flows from the fear of the Lord and leads to life and blessing; God’s commands are given for our good.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: obedience was the path to flourishing in the land. Now: walking in God’s ways remains the path of life and blessing for his people.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now this is the commandment—the statutes and the rules —that the LORD your God commanded me to teach you, that you may do them in the land to which you are going over, to possess it, that you may fear the LORD your God, you and your son and your son's son, by keeping all his statutes and his commandments, which I command you, all the days of your life, and that your days may be long. Hear therefore, O Israel, and be careful to do them, that it may go well with you, and that you may multiply greatly, as the LORD, the God of your fathers, has promised you, in a land flowing with milk and honey.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the great confession, Moses states what all of it is for: that you may fear the LORD your God, you and your son and your son’s son… and that your days may be long.

Three generations in one verse. Moses is a hundred and twenty and speaking to men in middle age about their grandchildren, and this is the horizon of the whole chapter. Nothing here is aimed only at the people in front of him.

And note what the law is said to produce: not merit, not standing, but life, and that it may go well with you, and multiplication in a land flowing with milk and honey. God is not restricting his people for the sake of restriction. Every command in this book is aimed at their flourishing, which is a claim the human heart has disbelieved since Eden and which is either true or it is not.

The word fear needs care, because it does not mean terror of a God who might turn on you. Deuteronomy uses it constantly and always alongside love and service and clinging. It is the awe of a creature standing in front of the living God and taking him seriously — the opposite of the casualness that treats him as a resource. A man who genuinely fears God in this sense is the freest man alive, because there is nothing else left in the world that can frighten him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–5 — The Shema: The Great Commandment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The central confession of Israel’s faith: the LORD is one, and he is to be loved with the whole heart, soul, and might. Jesus named this the greatest commandment.
verseByVerse.theology: God is one and demands undivided, whole-souled love. True religion is not mere ritual or doctrine but total love for the one true God, fulfilled in Christ and enabled by the Spirit.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel recited this morning and evening as the heart of their faith. Now: it remains the first and greatest commandment, the measure of all our love.

verseByVerse.quote: "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one.

These six Hebrew words are the most repeated sentence in the history of the Jewish people. They are said morning and evening, taught to children before they can read, written on the doorposts of houses, and were on the lips of countless Jews as they died. The whole faith of Israel is compressed into one line.

It opens with a command to listen. Not to think, or feel, or resolve — hear. Faith begins with somebody speaking and somebody attending. So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ (Rom. 10:17).

Then the confession, and the Hebrew is compressed almost to the point of ambiguity — literally the LORD our God, the LORD one. It carries at least two truths and Israel needed both. There is only one God, against a world with a god for every city, every crop and every crisis. And he is one — undivided, consistent, not at war with himself. The gods of the nations were a committee with rival interests, and a man could never know where he stood. Israel’s God has one will and one character, and he is the same on Tuesday as he was on the mountain.

Now, this is the verse Jewish objectors have always raised against the Trinity, and it should be answered rather than sidestepped. The word for one here is echad, which is not the word for mathematical singularity; it is the word used in Genesis 2:24 when a man and his wife become one flesh. It denotes united oneness, not solitary oneness. Christians confess exactly what this verse says — there is one God, and the Lord is one — and we say so in the words the New Testament itself uses when it takes the Shema and puts Jesus inside it: yet for us there is one God, the Father… and one Lord, Jesus Christ (1 Cor. 8:6). Paul did not abandon the Shema. He recited it, with a name in it.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might.

Of everything the one true God might have required first — sacrifice, obedience, worship, fear — what he asks for is love. And the Lord Jesus, asked to name the greatest commandment out of all six hundred and thirteen, quoted this verse (Mark 12:29–30) and said everything else hangs on it.

Take the three terms, because they are not a list of separate compartments; they are a way of saying everything three times over.

Heart in Hebrew is not the seat of the emotions but of the will and the thinking — the place where decisions get made. Soul is nephesh, the whole living self, your life as you actually live it. And might is me’od, an odd choice: it is normally an adverb meaning very or exceedingly. Loving God with all your very. The rabbis took it to include a man’s property, and they were probably right — your resources, your energy, your capacity, the whole of your muchness.

Which raises the obvious and crushing question. Who has ever done this? Not for a lifetime — for an hour. Nobody reading this has loved God with the whole of his will and life and capacity for a single morning.

And that is not a reason to lower the command; it is the reason the rest of the book exists. Deuteronomy will state the problem plainly (oh that they had such a heart, 5:29) and then announce the solution (the LORD your God will circumcise your heart… so that you will love the LORD your God with all your heart, 30:6). The commandment that exposes us is answered by a promise that God will do in us what he requires of us. Which is why John, who had lain against the chest of the Son of God, wrote the sentence that puts the Shema the right way round for a Christian: We love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–9 — These Words on the Heart: Passing Faith to Children
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s words are to be on the heart and taught diligently to children, woven into every moment of daily life — at home, on the road, lying down, rising up, bound on hand and forehead, written on doorposts.
verseByVerse.theology: Faith is to permeate the whole fabric of daily life and be deliberately handed to the next generation; the heart is the seat of true obedience.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: faith filled the Israelite home and journey. Now: Christian discipleship saturates ordinary life and is passed on through everyday, intentional instruction.

verseByVerse.quote: And these words that I command you today shall be on your heart. You shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And these words that I command you today shall be on your heart. You shall teach them diligently to your children.

Note the order, because it cannot be reversed. First on your heart, then teach them. A parent cannot hand on what he does not have; children are extraordinarily good at telling the difference between what their father believes and what he merely says on Sundays, and no amount of instruction survives that gap.

The verb behind teach diligently means to sharpen or to whet, as one sharpens a blade — repeatedly, with pressure, until an edge forms. It is not a single conversation.

And then Moses describes the method, and it is the least formal thing imaginable: talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise.

Sitting, walking, lying down, getting up. That is the whole of an ordinary day, from waking to sleeping, indoors and outdoors. There is no lesson slot here, no curriculum, no set hour. The faith is to be transmitted the way a family’s accent is transmitted — by constant, unremarkable exposure in the ordinary run of life.

Which is a relief and a rebuke at once. A relief, because it means a parent who is no teacher can still do this; the qualification is not eloquence but presence and honesty. A rebuke, because it cannot be delegated to a church or a school, and because the times listed are exactly the times most of us have handed over to a screen. What Moses describes is a household in which God comes up in conversation because he is genuinely on the mind of the people who live there.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall bind them as a sign on your hand, and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes. You shall write them on the doorposts of your house and on your gates.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You shall bind them as a sign on your hand, and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes. You shall write them on the doorposts of your house and on your gates.

Devout Jews have taken these words literally for well over two thousand years — the small leather boxes containing Scripture, bound to the arm and forehead for prayer, and the mezuzah fixed to the doorframe, touched on the way in and out. Whether Moses intended the literal practice or a vivid figure has been debated for centuries; what is not in doubt is what the four locations mean.

On your hand — what you do. Between your eyes — what you look at and think about. On the doorposts of your house — your private life, the place where nobody is watching. On your gates — the gate was where the town’s business was done, its cases tried and its deals struck; that is public life, work, and civic responsibility.

Hands, eyes, home, gates. There is no fifth category. God’s word is to govern a man’s actions, his attention, his household and his dealings in the world, and there is no area left over in which he may keep his own counsel.

And the Lord Jesus made one pointed remark about the practice, worth remembering here: some make their phylacteries broad (Matt. 23:5) — enlarging the boxes so everybody could see how seriously they took Scripture. The commandment can be obeyed to the letter and turned into its own opposite. The word was supposed to go on the hand so it would shape the hand, not so that people would look at the strap.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–15 — The Danger of Prosperity: Do Not Forget
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When Israel enters the good land full of houses, wells, and vineyards they did not build, they must beware of forgetting the LORD who redeemed them; he is a jealous God who tolerates no rivals.
verseByVerse.theology: Prosperity is a peculiar peril to faith; comfort breeds forgetfulness, and forgetfulness breeds idolatry. The fear of the Lord guards the heart in plenty.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel was warned not to forget God amid the gifts of the land. Now: affluence still dulls the soul, and we must remember the Giver behind every gift.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when the LORD your God brings you into the land that he swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, to give you—with great and good cities that you did not build, and houses full of all good things that you did not fill, and cisterns that you did not dig, and vineyards and olive trees that you did not plant—and when you eat and are full, then take care lest you forget the LORD, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the LORD your God brings you into the land… with great and good cities that you did not build, and houses full of all good things that you did not fill, and cisterns that you did not dig, and vineyards and olive trees that you did not plant — and when you eat and are full, then take care lest you forget the LORD.

Read the list again and count the phrase. Four times: that you did not build… did not fill… did not dig… did not plant. Moses hammers it, because everything Israel is about to own will be second-hand mercy. They will move into finished houses and drink from wells somebody else dug through rock and eat olives off trees that took fifteen years to come into bearing before they arrived.

And then the warning, and it is the great warning of this book: the danger is not adversity. It is when you eat and are full.

Consider the arithmetic of that. This nation survived slavery, plagues, a sea, a desert, serpents, plague, war and forty years of funerals with its faith more or less intact. Moses does not warn them about any of it. He warns them about full stomachs and good houses, and he is right — within a few generations of settling they are worshipping Baal.

Hardship drives people to God; comfort quietly persuades them they never needed him. And the mechanism is not rebellion but forgetting, which requires no decision at all. A man who prayed daily through an illness stops praying when he recovers, not because he has changed his mind about God but because the pressure that kept him on his knees has gone.

Which is why gratitude is not a nicety in the Christian life but a survival discipline. Every good thing in your house was given, and most of it was dug by somebody else. What do you have that you did not receive? (1 Cor. 4:7).

verseByVerse.quote: It is the LORD your God you shall fear. Him you shall serve and by his name you shall swear. You shall not go after other gods, the gods of the peoples who are around you— for the LORD your God in your midst is a jealous God— lest the anger of the LORD your God be kindled against you, and he destroy you from off the face of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is the LORD your God you shall fear. Him you shall serve and by his name you shall swear.

Fifteen centuries later, in a wilderness, a starving man quoted this verse to the devil.

Satan had offered the Lord Jesus all the kingdoms of the world for one act of worship, and the answer was: Be gone, Satan! For it is written, “You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve” (Matt. 4:10). He was quoting Deuteronomy 6:13. And when he was told to throw himself from the temple, he answered from verse 16 of this same chapter; and when he was told to turn stones into bread, from 8:3.

Every one of the three answers came from these chapters. When the Son of God was under maximum pressure, with no food and no company and the tempter in front of him, what came out of him was Deuteronomy. He had this book in him, and he used it — not by discussing, not by reasoning, but by quoting what was written and refusing to move off it.

Anybody who wonders whether memorising Scripture is a schoolroom exercise should sit with that. The Lord Jesus did not summon his divine authority in that desert. He used the same weapon available to any believer, and it was enough.

Verse 15 gives the reason for the exclusivity, and it is the language of marriage again: the LORD your God in your midst is a jealous God. Not a distant deity guarding his prerogatives, but one who is in your midst — living among them — and who will not share his wife with the gods of the neighbours.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–19 — Do Not Put the LORD to the Test
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses warns Israel not to test the LORD as they did at Massah, but to keep his commandments diligently, that it may go well with them as he drives out their enemies.
verseByVerse.theology: Faith trusts God rather than demanding proof; to test God is to doubt his goodness and faithfulness. Jesus wielded this verse against Satan.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel was warned against the unbelief of Massah. Now: faith rests in God’s promises rather than demanding signs; Christ models perfect trust.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not put the LORD your God to the test, as you tested him at Massah. You shall diligently keep the commandments of the LORD your God, and his testimonies and his statutes, which he has commanded you. And you shall do what is right and good in the sight of the LORD, that it may go well with you, and that you may go in and take possession of the good land that the LORD swore to give to your fathers by thrusting out all your enemies from before you, as the LORD has promised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You shall not put the LORD your God to the test, as you tested him at Massah.

Massah means testing, and the incident is in Exodus 17. There was no water, and the people quarrelled with Moses, and the place was named for the question they asked: Is the LORD among us or not? (Exod. 17:7).

Notice what testing God actually is, because it is easily confused with honest doubt. Scripture is full of people asking God hard questions, and he never once rebukes it — the Psalms are largely made of such questions. Testing is different. It is demanding that God prove himself on our terms, at our chosen moment, by a sign of our choosing, before we will go on trusting him. It puts God in the dock and the man on the bench.

And the reason it is so serious is what it implies about the past. Israel at Massah had watched the sea open. To say is the LORD among us or not after that is not a question; it is a verdict on everything he had already done, and it says that none of it counted.

This is the second verse in the chapter that the Lord Jesus used in the desert. When the devil quoted Scripture at him — throw yourself down, for it is written, “He will command his angels concerning you” — the answer was: Again it is written, “You shall not put the Lord your God to the test” (Matt. 4:7). Note what that exchange teaches. A verse can be quoted accurately and used wickedly, and the defence is not less Scripture but more of it, rightly related. The devil knows the Bible. He does not know it whole.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–25 — Tell the Story to Your Children
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When children ask the meaning of the commandments, parents are to rehearse the story of redemption — slavery in Egypt, the mighty deliverance, the gift of the land — so that faith is grounded in God’s saving acts.
verseByVerse.theology: Faith is transmitted through the retelling of redemption; obedience is the grateful response to God’s saving acts, never their cause.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israelite parents told the exodus story. Now: Christian parents tell the gospel story, grounding their children’s faith in what God has done in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "When your son asks you in time to come, 'What is the meaning of the testimonies and the statutes and the rules that the LORD our God has commanded you?' then you shall say to your son, 'We were Pharaoh's slaves in Egypt. And the LORD brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand. And the LORD showed signs and wonders, great and grievous, against Egypt and against Pharaoh and all his household, before our eyes. And he brought us out from there, that he might bring us in and give us the land that he swore to give to our fathers. And the LORD commanded us to do all these statutes, to fear the LORD our God, for our good always, that he might preserve us alive, as we are this day. And it will be righteousness for us, if we are careful to do all this commandment before the LORD our God, as he has commanded us.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends where the whole book is aimed: at a child’s question.

When your son asks you in time to come, “What is the meaning of the testimonies and the statutes and the rules that the LORD our God has commanded you?”

The scene is ordinary and every parent knows it. A boy grows up inside a household of habits he did not choose — the feasts, the Sabbath, the strange laws about mixed fabric and gleaning and firstfruits — and one day he asks why. It is the question that decides whether faith survives a generation, and Moses tells them exactly how to answer it.

Not with philosophy. Not with a defence of each individual statute. With a story: We were Pharaoh’s slaves in Egypt. And the LORD brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand.

That is the answer. Why do we live like this? Because of something that happened to us. We were slaves and we were rescued, and everything in this house follows from that one fact.

Notice the pronoun. We were Pharaoh’s slaves — said by a man whose parents came out of Egypt, to a boy who will be two generations further removed still. The rescue is not an event in the family’s past that they commemorate; it is the thing that happened to them, and each generation is taught to say so in the first person.

A Christian family answers the same question with the same shape. Why do we do this? Not because these are our standards, or our tradition, or how we were raised — but because we were slaves and were bought, at a price, by somebody who came for us. Any answer that does not put the rescue at the centre has already turned the faith into a set of house rules, and house rules do not survive a child leaving home.

6.theology:
The oneness of God and the love he demands. “The LORD our God, the LORD is one… you shall love the LORD your God with all your heart” (6:4–5). Because God is one and supreme, he claims undivided, whole-souled love. Jesus named this the greatest commandment (Mark 12:30); he alone fulfilled it, and by his Spirit the love of God is poured into our hearts (Rom 5:5).

Faith handed to the next generation. God’s words are to be on the heart and taught diligently in the rhythms of ordinary life (6:6–9), grounded in the retold story of redemption (6:20–25). Faith is always one generation from extinction; the remedy is deliberate, gospel-centered discipleship in the home.

The peril of prosperity. The great danger is not adversity but abundance: “take care lest you forget the LORD” (6:12). Comfort breeds forgetfulness, and forgetfulness breeds idolatry. The fear of the Lord and deliberate remembrance guard the heart in plenty.
6.examples:
Then: Israel was given the Shema as the heart of her faith — to love the one true God with everything, to weave that love into every moment of home and journey, to teach it diligently to her children, and to beware of forgetting God amid the gifts of the good land.

Now: The first and greatest commandment still measures our every love; we love God supremely only because Christ first loved the Father perfectly for us and pours his love into our hearts. We saturate ordinary life with the Word, tell our children the gospel story before the rules, resist the soul-dulling pull of affluence, and remember always the greater exodus by which the Lord Jesus brought us out of the house of our slavery to sin.

7.title: A Holy Nation: Chosen Not Because You Were Great, but Because He Loved You
7.text: <sup>1</sup>"When the LORD your God brings you into the land that you are entering to take possession of it, and clears away many nations before you, the Hittites, the Girgashites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, seven nations more numerous and mightier than you,<sup>2</sup>and when the LORD your God gives them over to you, and you defeat them, then you must devote them to complete destruction. You shall make no covenant with them and show no mercy to them.<sup>3</sup>You shall not intermarry with them, giving your daughters to their sons or taking their daughters for your sons,<sup>4</sup>for they would turn away your sons from following me, to serve other gods. Then the anger of the LORD would be kindled against you, and he would destroy you quickly.<sup>5</sup>But thus shall you deal with them: you shall break down their altars and dash in pieces their pillars and chop down their Asherim and burn their carved images with fire.<sup>6</sup>"For you are a people holy to the LORD your God. The LORD your God has chosen you to be a people for his treasured possession, out of all the peoples who are on the face of the earth.<sup>7</sup>It was not because you were more in number than any other people that the LORD set his love on you and chose you, for you were the fewest of all peoples,<sup>8</sup>but it is because the LORD loves you and is keeping the oath that he swore to your fathers, that the LORD has brought you out with a mighty hand and redeemed you from the house of slavery, from the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt.<sup>9</sup>Know therefore that the LORD your God is God, the faithful God who keeps covenant and steadfast love with those who love him and keep his commandments, to a thousand generations,<sup>10</sup>and repays to their face those who hate him, by destroying them. He will not be slack with one who hates him. He will repay him to his face.<sup>11</sup>You shall therefore be careful to do the commandment and the statutes and the rules that I command you today.<sup>12</sup>"And because you listen to these rules and keep and do them, the LORD your God will keep with you the covenant and the steadfast love that he swore to your fathers.<sup>13</sup>He will love you, bless you, and multiply you. He will also bless the fruit of your womb and the fruit of your ground, your grain and your wine and your oil, the increase of your herds and the young of your flock, in the land that he swore to your fathers to give you.<sup>14</sup>You shall be blessed above all peoples. There shall not be male or female barren among you or among your livestock.<sup>15</sup>And the LORD will take away from you all sickness, and none of the evil diseases of Egypt, which you knew, will he inflict on you, but he will lay them on all who hate you.<sup>16</sup>And you shall consume all the peoples that the LORD your God will give over to you. Your eye shall not pity them, neither shall you serve their gods, for that would be a snare to you.<sup>17</sup>"If you say in your heart, 'These nations are greater than I. How can I dispossess them?'<sup>18</sup>you shall not be afraid of them but you shall remember what the LORD your God did to Pharaoh and to all Egypt,<sup>19</sup>the great trials that your eyes saw, the signs, the wonders, the mighty hand, and the outstretched arm, by which the LORD your God brought you out. So will the LORD your God do to all the peoples of whom you are afraid.<sup>20</sup>Moreover, the LORD your God will send hornets among them, until those who are left and hide themselves from you are destroyed.<sup>21</sup>You shall not be in dread of them, for the LORD your God is in your midst, a great and awesome God.<sup>22</sup>The LORD your God will clear away these nations before you little by little. You may not make an end of them at once, lest the wild beasts grow too numerous for you.<sup>23</sup>But the LORD your God will give them over to you and throw them into great confusion, until they are destroyed.<sup>24</sup>And he will give their kings into your hand, and you shall make their name perish from under heaven. No one shall be able to stand against you until you have destroyed them.<sup>25</sup>The carved images of their gods you shall burn with fire. You shall not covet the silver or the gold that is on them or take it for yourselves, lest you be ensnared by it, for it is an abomination to the LORD your God.<sup>26</sup>And you shall not bring an abominable thing into your house and become devoted to destruction like it. You shall utterly detest and abhor it, for it is devoted to destruction.
7.overview:
Chapter 7 unfolds the doctrine of election in some of the tenderest words in all Scripture. Why did God choose Israel? Not because they were numerous (they were “the fewest of all peoples”), not because they were impressive or deserving — but simply “because the LORD loves you” (7:8). Election is rooted in nothing but the free, sovereign, unmerited love of God. Here is grace stripped of all human pretense.

The chapter opens with the hard command to destroy the seven nations of Canaan and to make no covenant or marriage with them, lest they turn Israel’s heart to idols. This “holy war” is not ethnic hatred but the judicial judgment of God upon peoples whose wickedness was complete, and a radical call to undivided devotion. Israel is to be a holy nation, set apart wholly to the LORD.

At the heart of the chapter shines the great covenant name: “the faithful God who keeps covenant and steadfast love with those who love him… to a thousand generations” (7:9). The God who chooses in love also keeps covenant in faithfulness.

The chapter ends with encouragement against fear: when Israel faces nations greater than themselves, they must remember the exodus and trust the God who is “in your midst, a great and awesome God” (7:21). Election, then, is no abstract doctrine but the unshakable ground of the believer’s assurance: we love because he first loved us.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel must devote the seven Canaanite nations to destruction and make no treaty or marriage with them, tearing down their altars, lest they be turned away to other gods.
verseByVerse.theology: God demands radical separation from idolatry; compromise with the world’s gods corrupts the heart and provokes God’s judgment.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel was to make no alliance with Canaanite idolatry. Now: believers are called to holy distinctness, refusing to be conformed to the idols of the age.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the LORD your God brings you into the land that you are entering to take possession of it, and clears away many nations before you, the Hittites, the Girgashites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, seven nations more numerous and mightier than you, and when the LORD your God gives them over to you, and you defeat them, then you must devote them to complete destruction. You shall make no covenant with them and show no mercy to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are among the hardest verses in the Bible, and they should be neither softened nor hurried past. You must devote them to complete destruction. You shall make no covenant with them and show no mercy to them.

The Hebrew word is herem: to devote something to God so completely that it is put beyond any human use. Applied to plunder it means burnt rather than kept. Applied to a people it means what it says.

Take first what the text itself supplies. The command is limited to seven named nations in one territory — the Hittites, the Girgashites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites. It is not a policy toward foreigners; the same book commands Israel to love the sojourner (10:19) and forbids her to abhor an Egyptian (23:7). It is bounded by geography, by a list, and by a moment.

Second, the reason, which Deuteronomy states repeatedly and which the reader has already met at 9:4–5 in advance: this is judicial. It is not because of your righteousness… but because of the wickedness of these nations that the LORD your God is driving them out. God had told Abraham four centuries earlier that his descendants would wait, for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete (Gen. 15:16) — which means God delayed judgment for four hundred years while a civilisation ripened. What ripened is described in the previous chapter of this commentary and in 12:31: they burned their children.

Third, and this must be said plainly: it is a model for nobody. No nation, church or individual since has held this commission, and the New Testament closes the door explicitly. My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting (John 18:36); the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh (2 Cor. 10:4). Every use of this chapter to justify violence has been a misuse.

And what remains after all that is still hard, and Scripture does not remove it. What is left is the question of whether God has the right to judge, and when. He does, and he exercises it in every generation without consulting us; what is unusual here is only that we are allowed to watch. Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just? (Gen. 18:25) — asked, note, by a man arguing with God about the destruction of cities, and asked as a confidence.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall not intermarry with them, giving your daughters to their sons or taking their daughters for your sons, for they would turn away your sons from following me, to serve other gods. Then the anger of the LORD would be kindled against you, and he would destroy you quickly. But thus shall you deal with them: you shall break down their altars and dash in pieces their pillars and chop down their Asherim and burn their carved images with fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Verses 3 to 5 tell us what the danger actually was, and it is not military.

You shall not intermarry with them… for they would turn away your sons from following me, to serve other gods.

There is the reason, stated by God himself. The prohibition is not racial — Deuteronomy has no interest in blood, and the Old Testament is full of outsiders brought in and honoured. Rahab was a Canaanite of Jericho and is in the genealogy of Christ. Ruth was a Moabite and is King David’s great-grandmother. Both married Israelites, and Scripture celebrates it. What made them different is not ancestry but that they had come over to the God of Israel — your people shall be my people, and your God my God (Ruth 1:16).

The danger is entirely religious, and God names the exact mechanism: not that the Israelite husband will be argued out of his faith, but that his sons will be raised by a mother who worships something else. It is a warning about the next generation, made two verses after a chapter about teaching children.

Paul applies the identical principle to the church, and gives the identical reason — not ethnicity but allegiance: a widow is free to remarry whom she wishes, only in the Lord (1 Cor. 7:39). It is one of those places where a command that sounds harsh in the abstract turns out to be a father protecting his grandchildren.

And then verse 5, which shows what the real war was: break down their altars and dash in pieces their pillars and chop down their Asherim and burn their carved images with fire. Israel is to destroy the shrines, not loot them. The campaign was against the worship, and Israel’s own history would prove why: every time she left a shrine standing, she ended up kneeling at it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–11 — Chosen in Love: The Heart of Election
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel is a holy people, God’s treasured possession, chosen not for their greatness but simply because God loved them and kept his oath to their fathers; he is the faithful God who keeps covenant to a thousand generations.
verseByVerse.theology: Election rests on God’s free, sovereign love alone, not on human merit; the chosen are kept by God’s covenant faithfulness.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel was God’s treasured possession by grace. Now: believers are a chosen people (1 Pet 2:9), saved not by works but by sovereign love.

verseByVerse.quote: "For you are a people holy to the LORD your God. The LORD your God has chosen you to be a people for his treasured possession, out of all the peoples who are on the face of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you are a people holy to the LORD your God. The LORD your God has chosen you to be a people for his treasured possession, out of all the peoples who are on the face of the earth.

Two words carry this verse.

Holy — qadosh — does not first mean morally pure. It means set apart, separated for a particular use. A holy pot in the tabernacle was not a better-behaved pot; it was a pot that could not be used for anything else. Israel is holy because God has taken her out of general circulation for himself.

And treasured possession is segullah, a word from the world of kings. A king had the wealth of the realm — the treasury, the taxes, the state property — and then he had his segullah: the private hoard he had gathered himself, kept apart from the national accounts, the things that were personally his. Everything belongs to God by right of creation; the earth is the LORD’s and the fullness thereof (Ps. 24:1). Israel is his in a different way, the way a man’s own things are his.

Peter takes both words, the whole verse, and hands them to a scattered congregation of Gentile Christians without alteration: But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession (1 Pet. 2:9). Everything said here of Israel he says of them, and the reason he can is in the next clause of his sentence — that you may proclaim the excellencies of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light.

verseByVerse.quote: It was not because you were more in number than any other people that the LORD set his love on you and chose you, for you were the fewest of all peoples, but it is because the LORD loves you and is keeping the oath that he swore to your fathers, that the LORD has brought you out with a mighty hand and redeemed you from the house of slavery, from the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now the two verses at the heart of the chapter, and there is nothing else quite like them in the Old Testament.

It was not because you were more in number than any other people that the LORD set his love on you and chose you, for you were the fewest of all peoples, but it is because the LORD loves you and is keeping the oath that he swore to your fathers.

Moses is answering the question every chosen person eventually asks: why me? And he demolishes the obvious answer first. It was not size. Israel was the fewest of all peoples — a small, late, insignificant nation with no civilisation to speak of, choosing to say so in its own Scriptures, which is not how nations write about themselves.

Nor was it goodness. Two chapters from now Moses will be blunter still: Know, therefore, that the LORD your God is not giving you this good land to possess because of your righteousness, for you are a stubborn people (9:6).

So what is left? Read the sentence again and watch it close the circle. It is because the LORD loves you — and if you ask why he loves them, the answer is: because he loves them. There is no term underneath it. God’s love for his people has no cause outside himself, which is precisely why nothing outside himself can end it.

Feel the weight of that for a moment. If God had chosen Israel for something in her, then that thing would have to be maintained, and the day it failed the choosing would fail with it. Every believer who has ever lain awake wondering whether God has finally had enough of him is asking whether the ground of his acceptance is in himself. This verse says it never was.

Paul says the same thing in the same shape, and adds the cost: God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Rom. 5:8). Not when we were promising. Not when the trend was upward. While we were still sinners — which is to say, at the point when there was nothing whatever in us to explain it.

verseByVerse.quote: Know therefore that the LORD your God is God, the faithful God who keeps covenant and steadfast love with those who love him and keep his commandments, to a thousand generations, and repays to their face those who hate him, by destroying them. He will not be slack with one who hates him. He will repay him to his face. You shall therefore be careful to do the commandment and the statutes and the rules that I command you today.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Know therefore that the LORD your God is God, the faithful God who keeps covenant and steadfast love with those who love him and keep his commandments, to a thousand generations, and repays to their face those who hate him.

The great covenant words all gather here. Faithful — ne’eman, from the root that gives us amen: reliable, firm, the sort of thing you can put your weight on. Steadfast love — chesed, the largest word in the Old Testament, meaning loyal covenant love that keeps going when the other party has given every reason to stop.

And then the arithmetic again, as in the second commandment: to a thousand generations against judgment repaid within a lifetime. A thousand generations at even twenty-five years apiece is twenty-five thousand years — which is a Hebrew way of saying: for ever, past any horizon you can see.

But do not skip verse 10, because Deuteronomy will not let the picture be sentimental. He repays to their face those who hate him. He will not be slack with one who hates him. The phrase to their face means directly, personally, not through intermediaries — and not slack means he does not let it drift. The same God is described in one breath as keeping love for a thousand generations and as settling accounts without delay, and a reader who takes only one half has not got the God of the Bible.

Then verse 11: You shall therefore be careful to do the commandment. There is the therefore again, and it is always in the same place. Because he chose you, because he loves you, because he is faithful — therefore obey. Never the other way round.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–16 — The Blessings of Covenant Faithfulness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: If Israel keeps the covenant, God will love and bless them above all peoples — fruitfulness of womb, field, and flock, and freedom from disease — and they must not pity the idols of the nations.
verseByVerse.theology: God delights to bless his covenant people; obedience flows into flourishing, and idolatry is a snare to be utterly rejected.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel was promised abundant blessing for faithfulness. Now: the believer’s true and lasting blessings are secured in Christ, the seed of Abraham.

verseByVerse.quote: "And because you listen to these rules and keep and do them, the LORD your God will keep with you the covenant and the steadfast love that he swore to your fathers. He will love you, bless you, and multiply you. He will also bless the fruit of your womb and the fruit of your ground, your grain and your wine and your oil, the increase of your herds and the young of your flock, in the land that he swore to your fathers to give you. You shall be blessed above all peoples. There shall not be male or female barren among you or among your livestock. And the LORD will take away from you all sickness, and none of the evil diseases of Egypt, which you knew, will he inflict on you, but he will lay them on all who hate you. And you shall consume all the peoples that the LORD your God will give over to you. Your eye shall not pity them, neither shall you serve their gods, for that would be a snare to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The blessing list is generous and concrete: love, multiplication, the fruit of your womb and the fruit of your ground, your grain and your wine and your oil, the increase of your herds and the young of your flock, and freedom from the evil diseases of Egypt, which you knew.

These are farm blessings — children, crops, cattle, health. God speaks to this people about what actually filled their days, and there is nothing embarrassing about it. He is not offering Israel a religious experience; he is offering rain and babies and a healthy flock.

Two cautions belong here, though, and the second matters more.

The first is that these promises are made to a nation, under a specific covenant, in a specific land, with obedience and blessing tied together in a way the New Testament does not simply transfer to individuals. Job’s friends made exactly that mistake and were rebuked by God for it (Job 42:7). A Christian who reads verse 15 as a guarantee of health has misread the document he is standing in.

The second is what the blessings are for. Verse 14 says Israel will be blessed above all peoples, which sounds like favouritism until you remember why this family was called in the first place: in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed (Gen. 12:3). The blessing was always a conduit, never a terminus. A nation flourishing under God in full view of the world was the plan, and the surrounding peoples were meant to look and ask.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–26 — Do Not Be Afraid: Remember What God Did
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When Israel fears the greater nations, they must remember the exodus and trust the LORD who is in their midst, a great and awesome God who will clear the nations away little by little; meanwhile they must utterly destroy idols.
verseByVerse.theology: Faith conquers fear by remembering God’s past deliverance; God works gradually yet surely, and idolatry is an accursed thing to be wholly rejected.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel faced nations greater than themselves. Now: the believer faces overwhelming odds, armed with the memory of God’s mighty acts in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you say in your heart, 'These nations are greater than I. How can I dispossess them?' you shall not be afraid of them but you shall remember what the LORD your God did to Pharaoh and to all Egypt, the great trials that your eyes saw, the signs, the wonders, the mighty hand, and the outstretched arm, by which the LORD your God brought you out. So will the LORD your God do to all the peoples of whom you are afraid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God now says out loud the thing Israel has not said out loud.

If you say in your heart, “These nations are greater than I. How can I dispossess them?”

Notice where the fear is located: in your heart. Not in the assembly, not to Moses — the private thought at three in the morning, the one nobody admits to because saying it would be disloyal. God quotes it back to them before they have said it, which is its own comfort. He is not waiting to be told.

And the fear is accurate. The nations are greater. Verse 1 said so — seven nations more numerous and mightier than you. God never argues that the odds are better than they look.

His answer is a discipline of memory: you shall remember what the LORD your God did to Pharaoh and to all Egypt, the great trials that your eyes saw, the signs, the wonders, the mighty hand, and the outstretched arm. Then the inference: So will the LORD your God do to all the peoples of whom you are afraid.

That is how Scripture consistently treats fear, and it is worth noticing that it is not positive thinking. Nobody is told to feel differently, or to minimise the enemy, or to look within. They are directed to a specific thing God did in the past, which they saw, and told to reason forward from it. Faith here is an argument with evidence in it, and the evidence is historical.

The Christian has better evidence still, and Paul draws the same inference from it in the same form: He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?
