Ferguson notes the profound foreshadowing: where the curse falls, there the altar of atonement stands. The only hope of a people under the curse of the law is the altar — the sacrifice that bears the curse. Even here, at the mountain of cursing, the gospel of atonement is present, pointing to the cross where the curse and the sacrifice would meet in the body of Christ.

sections.title: Today You Have Become the People of the LORD
sections.commentary:
Moses and the Levitical priests address all Israel: “Keep silence and hear, O Israel: this day you have become the people of the LORD your God. You shall therefore obey the voice of the LORD your God, keeping his commandments” (vv. 9–10). The covenant ceremony marks a decisive moment — a renewal and reaffirmation of Israel's identity as God's covenant people.

Notice the order, which is the gospel order throughout Scripture: “this day you have become the people of the LORD your God. You shall therefore obey.” Identity precedes obedience; belonging precedes duty. Israel does not obey in order to become God's people; they obey because they already are God's people. Sproul stressed this fundamental pattern of grace: God first claims us as his own, and obedience flows as the grateful response to that prior belonging, never as its cause. The indicative (“you have become”) grounds the imperative (“you shall obey”).

Calvin observes that the call to “keep silence and hear” summons the people to reverent attention before the word of God; the covenant is received in humble listening. Begg notes the tender solemnity of the moment — Israel is being reminded who they are, that their whole life now flows from their identity as the people of the LORD. For the believer, this is the very heart of Christian living: we obey not to earn God's favor but because, in Christ, we have already become the people of God. “You are a chosen race… God's own people” (1 Pet 2:9) — therefore live as such. Ferguson notes that the imperatives of the Christian life always rest on the indicatives of grace; we are summoned to become what God has already declared us to be in Christ. The believer's obedience is the joyful working out of an identity freely given by grace.

sections.title: The Tribes on the Mountains; the Curses Proclaimed
sections.commentary:
Moses arranges the great ceremony: six tribes stand on Mount Gerizim to pronounce the blessing, and six on Mount Ebal for the curse (vv. 12–13). The Levites then proclaim a series of specific curses to all the people, who respond to each with “Amen” — binding themselves corporately to the covenant. The curses target hidden and grievous sins: idolatry, dishonoring parents, moving a neighbor's landmark, misleading the blind, perverting justice for the vulnerable, sexual sins, violence, and bribery to shed innocent blood (vv. 15–25).

Strikingly, many of these are secret sins — the idol “made in secret” (v. 15), the one who “misleads a blind person on the road” (v. 18), the one who “strikes down his neighbor in secret” (v. 24). The curses reach into the hidden places of life, where no human eye sees but God sees all. Sproul observed that the covenant binds not only outward conduct but the secret heart; God's law penetrates to what is done in darkness. There is no escaping the all-seeing eye of God.

The repeated “Amen” from all the people is profoundly significant. By saying “Amen” to each curse, the whole nation publicly agrees that those who commit such sins justly fall under God's curse — they ratify the justice of the covenant sanctions and bind themselves to its terms. Calvin notes that this corporate “Amen” made the covenant binding and the people accountable; they could never claim ignorance or injustice. Ferguson observes that the people, in their “Amen,” pronounce judgment on the very sins they are all too capable of committing — a sobering act of self-condemnation. The ceremony exposes the impossibility of the people's situation: they bind themselves to a law they cannot perfectly keep, agreeing that the curse is just. The mountain of cursing thus prepares the heart for the gospel, for it reveals that all stand under the curse and need a Redeemer who can bear it for them.

sections.title: Cursed Be Everyone Who Does Not Keep the Whole Law
sections.commentary:
The series of curses culminates in a comprehensive, sweeping declaration: “Cursed be everyone who does not confirm the words of this law by doing them. And all the people shall say, ‘Amen'” (v. 26). This final curse gathers up all the rest. It is no longer aimed at this or that specific sin but at any failure to keep the whole law. The standard is total, comprehensive, perfect obedience — and the curse falls on everyone who falls short of it.

Paul seizes on this very verse to make one of the great arguments of the gospel: “For all who rely on works of the law are under a curse; for it is written, ‘Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them'” (Gal 3:10). The logic is devastating and liberating. The law demands perfect, comprehensive obedience; no sinner can render it; therefore everyone who relies on law-keeping for justification stands under the curse of verse 26. The law, far from being a ladder to heaven, becomes a chain of condemnation, shutting every mouth and proving all guilty before God (Rom 3:19–20).

This is the law doing its great and necessary work: it drives us out of all self-righteousness and into the arms of Christ. For the curse pronounced from Mount Ebal — the curse that falls on all who fail to keep the whole law — is the very curse that Christ bore for us. Paul continues: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us—for it is written, ‘Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree'” (Gal 3:13). Sproul exulted in this exchange: the curse we earned, Christ absorbed; the “Amen” of self-condemnation we pronounced, Christ answered with his own body on the tree. Begg notes the staggering grace: the mountain of cursing points straight to Calvary, where the curse was exhausted and the blessing of Abraham flows to all who believe. The law's last word is curse; the gospel's last word is Christ, who became the curse that we might receive the blessing.

27.theology:
The curse of the law drives us to Christ. “Cursed be everyone who does not confirm the words of this law by doing them” (27:26). Paul quotes this to prove that the law cannot justify, for it demands perfect, comprehensive obedience no sinner can render (Gal 3:10). The law's great work is to shut every mouth and drive us to Christ, “who redeemed us from the curse… by becoming a curse for us” (Gal 3:13) on the tree.

The altar at the mountain of cursing. The altar of atonement is built on Mount Ebal, the mountain of curse (27:5–7), of uncut stones untouched by human tools. Where the curse falls, there the altar of sacrifice stands — a profound foreshadowing of the cross, where the curse and the sacrifice met in the body of Christ.

Identity precedes obedience. “This day you have become the people of the LORD your God. You shall therefore obey” (27:9–10). Belonging precedes duty; Israel obeys because they are God's people, not to become them. The believer's obedience is the joyful working out of an identity freely given by grace (1 Pet 2:9).
27.examples:
Then: Israel ratified the covenant at Shechem — writing the law on stones, building an altar of sacrifice at the very mountain of cursing, and standing between Gerizim and Ebal to say ‘Amen’ to the curses, binding themselves to a law they could never perfectly keep and agreeing that the curse upon lawbreakers was just.

Now: The curse of verse 26 has done its work in us, shutting every mouth and driving us out of self-righteousness into the arms of Christ. For the very curse we earned by failing to keep the whole law, Christ bore in our place, becoming a curse for us on the tree. The mountain of cursing points straight to Calvary, where the curse was exhausted and the blessing of Abraham now flows to all who believe. We obey not to become God's people, but because, in Christ, we already are.

28.title: Blessings and Curses: The Covenant Consequences
28.text: <sup>1</sup>‘And if you faithfully obey the voice of the LORD your God... the LORD your God will set you high above all the nations of the earth. <sup>2</sup>And all these blessings shall come upon you and overtake you...’ <sup>15</sup>‘But if you will not obey... then all these curses shall come upon you and overtake you.’
28.overview:
Chapter 28 is the longest and one of the most awesome chapters in Deuteronomy — the great chapter of covenant consequences. Having set the blessing and the curse before Israel, Moses now spells them out in overwhelming detail: lavish blessings for obedience (vv. 1–14) and devastating, escalating curses for disobedience (vv. 15–68). The sheer disproportion — fourteen verses of blessing, fifty-four of curse — is itself a sobering warning of how seriously God regards covenant faithfulness.

The blessings are comprehensive: blessing in the city and the field, in offspring and harvest and herds, in coming in and going out, in victory over enemies and abundance of every kind. To obey God is to walk into a flood of his goodness, to be “set high above all the nations” as “the head, not the tail.”

The curses are correspondingly comprehensive and terrifying. They escalate from agricultural failure and disease to military defeat, madness, oppression, and finally — most chillingly — to siege, exile, and scattering among the nations. These curses read like a prophecy of Israel's actual history, fulfilled in the Assyrian and Babylonian captivities and beyond.

This chapter confronts us with the holiness and justice of God, who will not be mocked. Yet for the believer, its glory is this: every curse here listed was borne by Christ, who became a curse for us (Gal 3:13). On the cross, the Lord Jesus absorbed the full weight of the covenant curse — the darkness, the forsakenness, the wrath — so that all who trust him might receive instead the full flood of the covenant blessing. The curses of Deuteronomy 28 fell on Calvary, that the blessings might fall on us.

sections.title: The Blessings of Obedience: Overtaken by Goodness
sections.commentary:
The chapter opens with a torrent of blessing. If Israel “faithfully obey the voice of the LORD,” then “all these blessings shall come upon you and overtake you” (vv. 1–2). The image is vivid: the blessings will pursue and overtake the obedient like a flood they cannot outrun. Blessing in the city and the field, in the fruit of the womb and the ground and the herds, in the basket and the kneading bowl, in coming in and going out (vv. 3–6) — every sphere of life saturated with God's goodness.

God promises victory over enemies, abundant rain, full barns, and exaltation among the nations: “The LORD will make you the head and not the tail” (v. 13), “set you high above all the nations of the earth” (v. 1). To walk in obedience is to walk into the smile of God and the flood of his favor. Begg notes the lavishness — God is no miser; he delights to pour out good upon those who walk in his ways. The blessings are pressed down, shaken together, running over.

Calvin cautions us to read these temporal blessings rightly within the old covenant: they were real, but they pointed beyond themselves to the spiritual and eternal blessings secured in Christ. Sproul stressed the underlying principle — obedience and blessing, sin and curse, are woven into the moral fabric of God's universe; we reap what we sow (Gal 6:7). Yet the deepest truth is that no sinner can claim these blessings by his own obedience, for none obeys perfectly (ch. 27:26). The blessings are secured for us not by our works but by the perfect obedience of Christ, the true and faithful Israelite, who alone kept the law flawlessly and into whose obedience we are received by faith. In him, “every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places” (Eph 1:3) becomes ours — the blessings of the covenant flowing to us through the One who obeyed in our place.

sections.title: Set High Above the Nations: The Head, Not the Tail
sections.commentary:
God's blessing extends from the home and the field to Israel's standing among the nations. He promises victory over enemies who “shall come out against you one way and flee before you seven ways” (v. 7), blessing on barns and on all the work of their hands (v. 8), and establishment as “a people holy to himself” so that “all the peoples of the earth shall see that you are called by the name of the LORD” (vv. 9–10). The obedient people become a public testimony to the watching world of the goodness and presence of their God.

The crowning promises soar: “The LORD will make you the head and not the tail, and you shall only go up and not down” (v. 13). To walk in obedience is to be lifted high under the smile of God, abounding in prosperity, lending to many and borrowing from none (v. 12). Sproul stressed that these blessings reflect the moral order God has woven into his universe — obedience and flourishing are bound together — yet they are not earned wages so much as the overflow of fellowship with a generous God.

Begg notes the warmth of the divine generosity: God delights to do his people good and to exalt them before the nations for his own glory. Yet the believer must remember that no sinner can claim these blessings by his own obedience, for none obeys perfectly (27:26). They are secured for us by the perfect obedience of Christ, the true and faithful Israelite who alone kept the law flawlessly. Ferguson observes that in him “every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places” (Eph 1:3) becomes ours — the head-not-the-tail exaltation fulfilled supremely in our union with the exalted Christ, in whom we are raised up and seated with him in the heavenly places (Eph 2:6). The blessings of the covenant flow to us through the One who obeyed in our place.

sections.title: The Curses of Disobedience: Disease, Defeat, and Oppression
sections.commentary:
Then the tone darkens. If Israel “will not obey,” then “all these curses shall come upon you and overtake you” (v. 15) — the same pursuing, overtaking language, now turned to judgment. The curses mirror and reverse the blessings: cursed in the city and the field, in the womb and the ground, in coming in and going out (vv. 16–19). And they escalate with terrifying detail: disease, drought, blight, military defeat, madness, blindness, oppression, the loss of everything labored for, until “you shall be only oppressed and robbed continually, and there shall be no one to help you” (v. 29).

The curses pile up relentlessly — the heavens like bronze, the earth like iron (v. 23), defeat before enemies, betrothed wives and built houses lost to others, children given to a foreign people while the eyes fail with longing (vv. 30–32). Sproul stressed that we must not flinch from the severity of these curses; they reveal the holiness and justice of God, who will not be mocked, and the dreadful reality of covenant-breaking. The disproportion of curse to blessing — fifty-four verses to fourteen — is itself a measure of how gravely God regards the betrayal of his covenant love.

Calvin observed that these curses are not arbitrary cruelty but the just recompense of a people who spurn the God who redeemed them; the more lavish the love spurned, the more terrible the judgment incurred. And the curses serve as a merciful warning — set before the people precisely so they might be moved to obedience and life. Ferguson notes the sobering realism of Deuteronomy: God tells his people in advance exactly what their unfaithfulness will cost, withholding nothing. For the believer, this catalog of curses is a window into what sin truly deserves — and a backdrop against which the cross blazes all the brighter. Every curse here listed is what we earned; every one of them was borne by Christ, who absorbed the wrath of the broken covenant so that we might be spared.

sections.title: The Ultimate Curse: Siege, Exile, and Scattering
sections.commentary:
The curses reach their horrifying climax in the prophecy of siege, exile, and scattering. A nation “from far away” will swoop down “like the eagle” (v. 49), besieging the cities until, in the extremity of starvation, the people are driven to unspeakable horrors (vv. 52–57). Then comes the ultimate covenant reversal: “the LORD will scatter you among all peoples, from one end of the earth to the other” (v. 64), and — most chillingly — “the LORD will bring you back in ships to Egypt” (v. 68), undoing the exodus itself, returning the redeemed people to the house of bondage.

The tragedy is sharpened by the reason given for the curse: “because you did not serve the LORD your God with joyfulness and gladness of heart, because of the abundance of all things” (v. 47). The root of the curse is a joyless, ungrateful heart that took God's abundant blessings for granted and turned from him. Begg notes the searching diagnosis — it was not merely outward disobedience but the loss of joyful, grateful devotion that brought ruin. The peril of prosperity (ch. 8) comes home to roost.

These curses read like a prophecy of Israel's actual history — fulfilled in the Assyrian conquest of the northern kingdom, the Babylonian siege and exile of Judah, and the scattering of the Jewish people across the earth. Sproul stressed that the fulfillment of these curses in history vindicates the truthfulness of God's word; what Moses foretold came to pass with terrible precision. Yet even here, the deeper gospel truth shines. The exile and forsakenness that this chapter describes is precisely what Christ entered on the cross. He was driven out, scattered, forsaken — “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” — bearing the full curse of the broken covenant. Ferguson notes the staggering exchange: the Son of God endured the ultimate covenant curse of God-forsakenness so that we might never be forsaken. The curses of Deuteronomy 28 fell in their fullness on Calvary, that the blessings might fall on us.

28.theology:
Christ bore the covenant curse. The fifty-four verses of escalating curse — disease, defeat, siege, exile, forsakenness — reveal what sin truly deserves. Yet every curse here was borne by Christ, who “became a curse for us” (Gal 3:13). On the cross he absorbed the full weight of the broken covenant, even the ultimate curse of God-forsakenness (“why have you forsaken me?”), so that all who trust him might receive instead the full flood of the covenant blessing.

The holiness and justice of God. God will not be mocked; we reap what we sow (Gal 6:7). The terrifying severity of the curses, and their precise fulfillment in Israel's exile, vindicate the truthfulness of God's word and the gravity of spurning his covenant love. The disproportion of curse to blessing measures how seriously God regards covenant faithfulness.

The peril of joyless prosperity. The root of the curse was failing to serve God “with joyfulness and gladness of heart, because of the abundance of all things” (28:47). Ingratitude amid blessing is the seedbed of ruin — a sobering warning against taking God's goodness for granted.
28.examples:
Then: Israel heard set before them the flood of covenant blessing for obedience and the terrifying, escalating catalog of curses for disobedience — disease, defeat, siege, exile, and scattering — curses that would be fulfilled with awful precision in their later history because they did not serve God with joyful, grateful hearts amid abundance.

Now: We read this chapter as a window into what our sin deserves and a backdrop against which the cross blazes all the brighter. Every curse here listed fell upon Christ, who bore the wrath of the broken covenant — even the ultimate forsakenness — so that we might never be forsaken and might receive instead every spiritual blessing in him. The curses of Deuteronomy 28 fell on Calvary, that the blessings might fall on us. Let us serve our God with joyfulness and gladness of heart, never taking his abundant grace for granted.

29.title: The Covenant Renewed in Moab: The Secret Things Belong to God
29.text: <sup>4</sup>But to this day the LORD has not given you a heart to understand or eyes to see or ears to hear. <sup>29</sup>The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children forever, that we may do all the words of this law.
29.overview:
Chapter 29 opens the third and final address of Moses (chs. 29–30), in which the covenant is solemnly renewed on the plains of Moab before Israel enters the land. Moses gathers the whole nation — leaders and laborers, men, women, children, and sojourners — to “enter into the sworn covenant of the LORD your God” (29:12), binding not only the present generation but those “who are not here with us today” (29:15).

The chapter contains one of the most penetrating diagnoses of the human condition in all of Scripture: though Israel had seen God's mighty acts with their own eyes for forty years, “to this day the LORD has not given you a heart to understand or eyes to see or ears to hear” (29:4). The problem is not lack of evidence but a heart that cannot perceive — a spiritual blindness that only God can heal. This sets up the new covenant promise of chapter 30.

Moses warns solemnly against the secret apostate who, hearing the covenant curses, blesses himself in his heart, presuming he will be safe while walking in stubbornness. Such hidden rebellion will not escape God's notice or judgment, and Moses foresees the desolation of the land and the bewilderment of the nations at Israel's ruin.

The chapter closes with one of the great verses of Scripture: “The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us” (29:29). We are not to pry into God's hidden counsels but to obey what he has plainly revealed. Here is the wise boundary of all true faith — humble trust in God's sovereignty, joined to faithful obedience to his Word.

sections.title: Remember What Your Eyes Have Seen
sections.commentary:
Moses calls Israel to remember all that the LORD did before their eyes in Egypt and the wilderness — “the great trials that your eyes saw, the signs, and those great wonders” (v. 3). For forty years God had sustained them miraculously: “your clothes have not worn out on you, and your sandals have not worn off your feet” (v. 5). They had every reason to trust and obey.

And yet comes the arresting verse: “But to this day the LORD has not given you a heart to understand or eyes to see or ears to hear” (v. 4). Here is one of the most penetrating diagnoses of the human condition in Scripture. Despite four decades of overwhelming evidence — miracles, provision, judgment, deliverance — Israel still did not truly perceive. Why? Not for lack of evidence but for lack of a heart to understand. Sproul stressed the radical implication: the human problem is not fundamentally intellectual but spiritual; we are blind, deaf, and dull of heart by nature, unable to perceive the things of God until he gives us the capacity. Evidence alone cannot cure spiritual blindness.

Calvin saw here the foundation of the doctrine of regeneration: God must give “a heart to understand,” for the natural heart cannot grasp spiritual reality. This is exactly what Jesus would teach Nicodemus — “unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John 3:3) — and what Paul declares: “The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God… he is not able to understand them because they are spiritually discerned” (1 Cor 2:14). Ferguson notes that this verse cries out for the new covenant promise that follows in chapter 30, where God himself will circumcise the heart. The very thing Israel lacks — a heart to understand — is what God will sovereignly give. The chapter thus exposes our deep need and prepares us for the gospel: we cannot save ourselves or even truly see until God opens our eyes and gives us a new heart by his Spirit.

sections.title: Entering the Sworn Covenant: All the People Bound
sections.commentary:
Moses gathers the entire nation to enter into the covenant: “all of you… your heads, your tribes, your elders, and your officers, all the men of Israel, your little ones, your wives, and the sojourner who is in your camp, from the one who chops your wood to the one who draws your water” (vv. 10–11). No one is excluded — leader and laborer, man, woman, child, and even the foreigner. The covenant embraces the whole community in all its diversity.

And remarkably, the covenant binds not only those present but future generations: “it is not with you alone that I am making this sworn covenant… but with… whoever is not here with us today” (vv. 14–15). The covenant reaches forward through time, binding children yet unborn. Calvin notes the generational character of God's covenant dealings; God establishes his covenant with families and their descendants, “to a thousand generations” (7:9). The covenant is not a private transaction but a corporate, generational bond.

The inclusion of the lowliest — the woodcutter and the water-drawer — alongside the leaders teaches that all stand equally before God in covenant. Begg notes the beautiful equality: in the covenant, the servant and the prince stand on level ground, both equally claimed by God and equally bound to him. Ferguson observes that this points to the new covenant people, gathered from every station, “from the least of them to the greatest” (Heb 8:11), Jew and Gentile, slave and free, male and female, all one in Christ. The God who gathered the whole nation into covenant on the plains of Moab is the God who gathers a people from every tribe and tongue into the new covenant sealed in Christ's blood — a covenant that embraces us and our children, binding generation to generation in the bonds of grace.

sections.title: The Secret Apostate and the Desolation of the Land
sections.commentary:
Moses warns solemnly against a particular danger: the secret apostate. There may be among them someone “whose heart is turning away today from the LORD,” who, on hearing the covenant curses, “blesses himself in his heart, saying, ‘I shall be safe, though I walk in the stubbornness of my heart'” (vv. 18–19). This is the person who presumes upon grace while secretly clinging to sin — outwardly part of the covenant community, inwardly rebellious, imagining that he will escape judgment.

God's response is fearsome: “The LORD will not be willing to forgive him… and the LORD will blot out his name from under heaven” (v. 20). Sproul stressed the deadly danger of presumption — the false security of one who hears the warnings of God's word and yet hardens his heart, assuming the curse will not touch him. There is no more dangerous spiritual condition than to sit under the gospel while secretly nursing rebellion, presuming on grace while refusing repentance. Calvin warns that such self-deception, this “blessing of oneself” in sin, provokes God's particular anger, for it despises both his warnings and his mercy.

Moses then foresees the desolation of the land — brimstone and salt, a burning waste like Sodom and Gomorrah — and the bewilderment of the nations who will ask, “Why has the LORD done thus to this land?” And the answer: “It is because they abandoned the covenant of the LORD” (vv. 24–25). Ferguson notes the sobering public witness of judgment; Israel's ruin would testify to the nations of the seriousness of forsaking God. For the believer, this passage searches the heart: are we, perhaps, secret apostates, hearing the word yet presuming on grace while clinging to cherished sin? The warning is a means of grace, calling us to genuine repentance and warning us never to bless ourselves in our sin, for the all-seeing God knows the secret turnings of every heart.

sections.title: The Secret Things and the Revealed Things
sections.commentary:
The chapter closes with one of the great and treasured verses of Scripture: “The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children forever, that we may do all the words of this law” (v. 29). This single verse draws a wise and liberating boundary around all human inquiry into the ways of God.

There are “secret things” — the hidden counsels, the inscrutable purposes, the mysteries of God's sovereign will that he has not chosen to disclose. These “belong to the LORD”; they are his alone, and we are not to pry into them or demand explanations for what God has not revealed. Sproul, who loved this verse, stressed the humility it teaches: there are things we cannot know and are not meant to know, and faith rests content in the goodness and wisdom of God even where his ways are hidden. We do not need to penetrate the secret will of God; we need only trust the God whose secret will is always wise and good.

But there are also “the things that are revealed,” which “belong to us and to our children forever” — and the purpose of revelation is not mere knowledge but obedience: “that we may do all the words of this law.” Calvin draws out the balance: we are not to be idle speculators about God's hidden decrees but diligent doers of his revealed will. God has told us all we need to know and do; the rest we leave humbly in his hands. Ferguson notes the pastoral comfort: when we face the inexplicable — suffering, providence, the mysteries of God's dealings — we rest in the truth that the secret things belong to the Lord, while we devote ourselves to obeying what he has plainly revealed. This is the posture of mature faith: humble trust in God's sovereignty over what we cannot understand, joined to faithful obedience to what he has clearly made known. Where God has spoken, we obey; where God is silent, we trust.

29.theology:
The need for a new heart. Despite forty years of miracles, “the LORD has not given you a heart to understand or eyes to see or ears to hear” (29:4). The human problem is not lack of evidence but spiritual blindness; evidence cannot cure a heart that cannot perceive. This cries out for regeneration — the new covenant promise (ch. 30) that God himself will give the heart we lack (John 3:3; 1 Cor 2:14).

The danger of presumption. The secret apostate “blesses himself in his heart, saying, ‘I shall be safe, though I walk in the stubbornness of my heart'” (29:19). To presume on grace while clinging to sin is the most dangerous spiritual condition; the all-seeing God knows every secret turning of the heart and calls us to genuine repentance.

The secret and the revealed. “The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us… that we may do all the words of this law” (29:29). Mature faith trusts God's sovereignty over what we cannot understand and obeys what he has plainly revealed. Where God has spoken, we obey; where God is silent, we trust.
29.examples:
Then: Moses renewed the covenant on the plains of Moab, binding the whole nation and generations to come, diagnosing Israel's deep need of a heart to understand, warning against the secret apostate who presumes on grace, and teaching that the secret things belong to God while the revealed things are given for obedience.

Now: We confess our own deep need — that we were spiritually blind until God gave us a heart to understand and eyes to see, the very gift promised in the new covenant and given in the Spirit. We heed the warning against presuming on grace while nursing secret sin, and we embrace the wise boundary of faith: trusting God's sovereign goodness over all that is hidden, while devoting ourselves to obeying all that he has plainly revealed in his Word.

30.title: The Promise of Restoration: God Will Circumcise Your Heart
30.text: <sup>6</sup>And the LORD your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring, so that you will love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul, that you may live. <sup>14</sup>But the word is very near you. It is in your mouth and in your heart, so that you can do it. <sup>19</sup>...choose life...
30.overview:
Chapter 30 is the glorious turning point of Deuteronomy's final addresses, blazing with gospel hope. After the dark catalog of curses and the sober diagnosis of Israel's heartlessness, Moses now looks beyond the inevitable failure and exile to a day of restoration — and to the deepest promise of all: that God himself will transform the heart his people cannot change.

Moses foresees that the curses will come, Israel will be scattered, and then — “when all these things come upon you… and you return to the LORD your God” (30:1–2) — God will restore their fortunes, gather them from exile, and bring them home. But the heart of the chapter is verse 6: “the LORD your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring, so that you will love the LORD your God with all your heart.” What the law commanded in 10:16 (“circumcise your heart”) but could not produce, God now promises to accomplish himself. This is the new covenant — the very heart of the gospel.

The chapter then declares that this word is not far off or unattainable: “the word is very near you. It is in your mouth and in your heart, so that you can do it” (30:14). Paul takes up this very passage in Romans 10 to describe the nearness and accessibility of the gospel — the righteousness of faith, received not by climbing to heaven but by the word that is near.

Finally, Moses sets before Israel the great choice: “I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse. Therefore choose life” (30:19). With heaven and earth as witnesses, he pleads with his people to love the LORD, obey his voice, and hold fast to him — for he is their life and the length of their days.

sections.title: Restoration After Exile: The God Who Gathers
sections.commentary:
Moses looks beyond the curses and the exile to a day of restoration. “When all these things come upon you, the blessing and the curse… and you return to the LORD your God… then the LORD your God will restore your fortunes and have mercy on you, and he will gather you again from all the peoples where the LORD your God has scattered you” (vv. 1–3). The same God who scatters in judgment gathers in mercy. Exile is not the last word.

This is breathtaking grace. Even as Moses foretells the inevitable failure of Israel, he already proclaims the certainty of their restoration. Begg notes the pattern that runs through all of Scripture: God's judgments on his covenant people are never final; beyond every exile lies a homecoming, beyond every scattering a gathering. The God of Deuteronomy is the God of return, the God who, having disciplined his wayward children, will surely bring them home. Calvin observes that this promise rests not on Israel's faithfulness but on God's mercy and his covenant commitment; he gathers them “from the uttermost parts of heaven” (v. 4) because he will not abandon his own.

The note of repentance — “you return to the LORD your God” — is essential, yet even this return, the next verses will reveal, is ultimately God's own work in the heart. Sproul stressed that the restoration is grounded in the mercy of God, who delights to forgive and gather his scattered people. Ferguson notes that this promise of regathering finds its deepest fulfillment in the gospel, as Christ gathers his scattered sheep from every nation (John 11:52) into one flock. The God who promised to gather exiled Israel is the God who, in Christ, gathers all his lost and wandering people home to himself. No exile is so distant, no scattering so complete, that God's gathering mercy cannot reach it.

sections.title: The LORD Will Circumcise Your Heart: The New Covenant
sections.commentary:
Here is the mountain peak of Deuteronomy, the verse toward which the whole book has been climbing: “And the LORD your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring, so that you will love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul, that you may live” (v. 6). Everything converges here. In 10:16, Israel was commanded, “Circumcise your heart” — but they could not do it; the stubborn heart cannot cut itself. In 29:4, Moses diagnosed the problem: they had no heart to understand. Now, gloriously, God promises to do himself what he had commanded and they could not perform: “the LORD your God will circumcise your heart.”

This is the new covenant in its very essence — the heart of the gospel proclaimed in shadow centuries before Christ. What the law could not accomplish, God himself will accomplish by sovereign grace. He will cut away the hardness, renew the heart, and create within his people the very love he demands. The Shema's command — “love the LORD your God with all your heart” (6:5) — which no sinner could fulfill, will be made possible by God's own act of heart-transformation. Sproul exulted in this: God does not merely demand a new heart; he gives one. This is monergistic grace — God working alone to regenerate the heart.

The prophets would unfold this same promise: “I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you” (Ezek 36:26); “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts” (Jer 31:33). And the New Testament declares it fulfilled: “circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit” (Rom 2:29). Ferguson notes the wonder — the love that Deuteronomy commands from beginning to end is finally given as a gift, worked in the heart by the Spirit through the finished work of Christ. Begg observes that here the gospel breaks through the law: salvation is God's work from first to last, for he gives the very heart that loves and obeys him. What we could never do, God does for us and in us. This is grace upon grace.

sections.title: The Word Is Very Near You
sections.commentary:
Moses now declares the nearness and accessibility of God's word: “For this commandment that I command you today is not too hard for you, neither is it far off. It is not in heaven, that you should say, ‘Who will ascend to heaven for us and bring it to us…?' Neither is it beyond the sea… But the word is very near you. It is in your mouth and in your heart, so that you can do it” (vv. 11–14). God's word is not a remote, unattainable thing requiring heroic effort to reach; it is near, given, accessible.

Paul seizes on this very passage in Romans 10 and applies it to the gospel of justification by faith: “Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will ascend into heaven?' (that is, to bring Christ down) or ‘Who will descend into the abyss?' (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead)… But what does it say? ‘The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart' (that is, the word of faith that we proclaim)” (Rom 10:6–8). Sproul stressed the profound point Paul draws out: we do not save ourselves by some heroic ascent to heaven or descent to the depths; the work is already done, and the word of salvation is near, to be received by faith. We need not climb to God, for in Christ God has come near to us.

In the context of Deuteronomy, this nearness is bound up with the heart-circumcision just promised — for it is precisely when God circumcises the heart that his word becomes truly near, in mouth and heart, “so that you can do it.” Ferguson notes the connection: the word can only be in the heart and obeyed by those whose hearts God has renewed. The gospel is gloriously accessible — not a burden to be hauled down from heaven by our striving, but a gift to be received where we are. Christ has come down, has risen, has accomplished it all; the word of faith is near you. Begg observes the comfort: salvation is not a distant, impossible achievement but a near and present gift, as near as the word in your mouth and the faith in your heart.

sections.title: Choose Life
sections.commentary:
The chapter — and the whole sweep of covenant exhortation — climaxes in Moses' impassioned plea: “See, I have set before you today life and good, death and evil… therefore choose life, that you and your offspring may live, loving the LORD your God, obeying his voice and holding fast to him, for he is your life and length of your days” (vv. 15, 19–20). With heaven and earth called as witnesses, Moses sets the great choice before his people and pleads with all his heart: choose life.

This is the climactic appeal of Deuteronomy. The whole book has set forth the two ways — the way of love and obedience that leads to life and blessing, and the way of rebellion that leads to death and curse. Now Moses, with the urgency of a dying father, presses the choice home. Sproul noted the beautiful gathering of the book's great themes in the call: love the LORD, obey his voice, hold fast to him — for “he is your life.” Life is not merely the reward of choosing rightly; God himself is the life. To choose life is to choose the LORD.

How does this earnest call to “choose life” relate to the sovereign promise of heart-circumcision in verse 6? Ferguson and the Reformed tradition hold these together without contradiction: God's sovereign work in the heart does not cancel human responsibility but enables it. The God who commands “choose life” is the God who gives the new heart that makes the choosing possible; his grace does not remove the call but empowers the response. Calvin saw no tension here — the appeal is sincere and the responsibility real, even as the enabling is God's gift. Begg notes the tender earnestness of Moses' plea, echoing the heart of God himself who “desires all people to be saved” (1 Tim 2:4) and who pleads, “Why will you die? … Turn, and live” (Ezek 18:31–32). For the believer and for every hearer of the gospel, the call still sounds with all its urgency: choose life. Love the Lord, obey his voice, hold fast to him — for he is your life, and in Christ, the giver of the new heart, that life is freely offered to all who come.

30.theology:
The new covenant: God circumcises the heart. “The LORD your God will circumcise your heart… so that you will love the LORD your God with all your heart” (30:6). What the law commanded (10:16) but could not produce, God promises to accomplish himself. This is the heart of the gospel — what we could never do, God does for us and in us by his Spirit (Ezek 36:26; Jer 31:33; Rom 2:29). Salvation is God's sovereign work from first to last.

The word is very near. The word “is in your mouth and in your heart, so that you can do it” (30:14). Paul applies this to the gospel of faith (Rom 10:6–8): we do not save ourselves by ascending to heaven or descending to the depths; Christ has done it all, and the word of salvation is near, received by faith. We need not climb to God, for in Christ God has come near to us.

Choose life. “I have set before you life and death… therefore choose life… for he is your life” (30:19–20). God's sovereign work in the heart does not cancel human responsibility but enables it; the God who commands the choice gives the new heart that makes it possible. The earnest call still sounds to all: choose life by holding fast to the Lord, who is himself our life.
30.examples:
Then: Moses looked beyond the inevitable curse and exile to the certainty of restoration, promised that God himself would circumcise the hardened heart his people could not change, declared the word near and accessible, and pleaded with all his heart that Israel would choose life by loving and holding fast to the Lord.

Now: We rejoice that the promise of the circumcised heart is fulfilled in the new covenant: what we could never do, God has done for us and in us by his Spirit, giving us a new heart that loves him. The gospel is near — Christ has come down, has risen, has accomplished it all — and the word of faith is as near as our mouths and hearts. And the call still sounds with all its urgency to every soul: choose life; love the Lord, obey his voice, hold fast to him, for he is your life and the length of your days.

31.title: Moses' Farewell and the Law Deposited
31.text: <sup>6</sup>‘Be strong and courageous. Do not fear or be in dread of them, for it is the LORD your God who goes with you. He will not leave you or forsake you.’ <sup>8</sup>‘It is the LORD who goes before you. He will be with you; he will not leave you or forsake you. Do not fear or be dismayed.’
31.overview:
Chapter 31 begins the closing scenes of Deuteronomy and of Moses' life. At a hundred and twenty years old, Moses prepares to die, and the great transitions of leadership and covenant take place. He publicly commissions Joshua, deposits the written law beside the ark, and — sobering as it is — receives God's prediction that Israel will, after his death, turn to apostasy.

The chapter's golden thread is the promise of God's faithful presence. To all Israel and then to Joshua, Moses gives the great charge that will echo into the book of Joshua and through all of Scripture: “Be strong and courageous… for it is the LORD your God who goes with you. He will not leave you or forsake you” (31:6, 8). The courage of God's people rests not on their own strength but on the unfailing presence of God.

Moses writes down the law and commands it to be read publicly every seventh year, so that every generation — including children and sojourners — will hear and learn to fear the LORD. The Word is to be preserved, deposited, and continually proclaimed.

Yet the chapter is shadowed by realism. God tells Moses plainly that Israel will forsake the covenant and turn to other gods, and he commands the Song of Moses (chapter 32) to be written as a witness against them. Even as leadership passes and the future opens, God knows the hearts of his people and provides, in his word, a testimony that will outlast their unfaithfulness — and point beyond it to his own faithfulness.

sections.title: Be Strong and Courageous: God Goes With You
sections.commentary:
Moses, now a hundred and twenty, announces that he can no longer lead and will not cross the Jordan (vv. 1–2). But the work will go on, for “the LORD your God himself will go over before you” (v. 3). And to all Israel he gives the great charge: “Be strong and courageous. Do not fear or be in dread of them, for it is the LORD your God who goes with you. He will not leave you or forsake you” (v. 6). Then he repeats it to Joshua personally: “It is the LORD who goes before you. He will be with you; he will not leave you or forsake you. Do not fear or be dismayed” (v. 8).

Here is one of the most cherished promises in all of Scripture, and notice its foundation: the courage commanded is grounded entirely in the presence of God. “Be strong and courageous” — why? Not because Israel is mighty or Joshua is capable, but “for it is the LORD your God who goes with you.” Sproul stressed that biblical courage is never self-confidence but God-confidence; it rests not on our resources but on his unfailing presence. The antidote to fear is the assurance that God goes with us and before us.

The promise “He will not leave you or forsake you” reverberates through Scripture. God repeats it to Joshua (Josh 1:5), and the writer of Hebrews applies it directly to every believer: “he has said, ‘I will never leave you nor forsake you.' So we can confidently say, ‘The Lord is my helper; I will not fear'” (Heb 13:5–6). Begg observes the tender comfort: the same promise given to Israel on the brink of the conquest is given to us in every trial — God will never abandon his own. Ferguson notes that this is the very presence secured for us by Christ, who promised, “I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matt 28:20), and whose name is Immanuel, God with us. The believer faces every fear, every battle, every uncertain future with the same unshakable ground of courage: the Lord himself goes with us and before us, and he will never leave us nor forsake us.

sections.title: The Law Deposited and Read Every Seven Years
sections.commentary:
Moses writes down “this law” and entrusts it to the Levitical priests and the elders, commanding that it be read aloud publicly before all Israel every seventh year at the Feast of Booths (vv. 9–11). The whole nation is to gather — “the men, women, and little ones, and the sojourner within your towns” — that they may “hear and learn to fear the LORD your God,” and that “their children, who have not known it, may hear and learn” (vv. 12–13).

The writing and depositing of the law underscores its permanence and authority; God's covenant word is preserved in writing, not left to the vagaries of memory or the inventions of men. Sproul stressed the importance of the written word — Scripture as God's enduring, authoritative revelation, deposited and preserved for all generations. The law is not a private possession of the priests but the inheritance of the whole people, to be read in their hearing.

The command for public reading every seven years reveals God's concern that every generation hear his word. Calvin notes the generational vision again at work: the children “who have not known it” must hear and learn, lest the faith die out for lack of teaching. The public reading of Scripture was the great means by which the covenant was kept alive in the nation's memory and the fear of the LORD was passed on. Begg observes the timeless principle: the people of God are sustained by the public reading and proclamation of his word; faith comes by hearing (Rom 10:17). This is why Paul charges Timothy, “devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture” (1 Tim 4:13). Ferguson notes that the inclusion of all — men, women, children, sojourners — shows that God's word is for the whole covenant community, none excluded. The believer treasures the written, preserved, publicly proclaimed word of God as the means by which the fear of the Lord is taught and passed from generation to generation, the abiding witness that outlasts every leader and every age.

sections.title: God's Prediction of Israel's Apostasy
sections.commentary:
As Moses and Joshua present themselves at the tent of meeting, God appears in the pillar of cloud and speaks a sobering prophecy: “this people will rise and whore after the foreign gods among them in the land… and forsake me and break my covenant” (v. 16). God knows, before Israel even enters the land, that they will turn away. And he tells Moses the judgment that will follow: “my anger will be kindled against them… and I will hide my face from them” (v. 17).

This is a striking and sobering disclosure. God does not enter into covenant with Israel under any illusion about their faithfulness; he knows in advance that they will forsake him. Sproul observed the profound realism of this — God's foreknowledge of human sin does not diminish his commitment to his people, nor does it make him the author of their sin. He knows the hearts of his people fully, and still he loves and covenants with them. Calvin notes that this foreknowledge magnifies both the patience of God, who bears with a people he knows will betray him, and the responsibility of Israel, who sin against full light.

In response, God commands Moses to write the Song (chapter 32) as a witness against them: “that this song may be a witness for me against the people of Israel” (v. 19). Even Israel's coming apostasy is met with God's provision — a song that will testify to his faithfulness and their unfaithfulness, preserved in their own mouths. Ferguson notes the grace hidden in the severity: God provides, in advance, a witness that will call his wayward people back, a word that will outlast their rebellion. The God who foreknows our failures provides, even before they occur, the means of our recall and restoration. And ultimately, this points to the gospel: God, knowing fully the depth of our sin and betrayal before the foundation of the world, set his love upon us anyway and provided in Christ the remedy for the very unfaithfulness he foresaw.

sections.title: The Law as a Witness; Moses Finishes His Work
sections.commentary:
God commissions Joshua directly: “Be strong and courageous, for you shall bring the people of Israel into the land that I swore to give them. I will be with you” (v. 23). The same charge given through Moses is now confirmed by God himself, with the same ground — “I will be with you.” The mantle passes, but the promise of presence remains constant.

Moses finishes writing the words of the law “to the very end” and commands the Levites to place the Book of the Law “by the side of the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God, that it may be there for a witness against you” (vv. 24–26). The deposited law stands as a permanent testimony — a witness to God's revealed will and against the people's disobedience. Sproul noted the solemn function of the written word: it testifies for God and against human sin, an objective standard that cannot be altered or evaded. Calvin observes that the law beside the ark, like the song in their mouths, ensured that Israel could never plead ignorance of God's covenant.

Moses' final words in this chapter are heavy with realistic sorrow: “I know how rebellious and stubborn you are… how much more after my death!” (v. 27). He gathers the elders to recite the Song that will follow, knowing that “you will surely act corruptly and turn aside from the way that I have commanded you” (v. 29). Begg notes the pathos of these closing words — the aged shepherd, having poured out his life for this people, knows they will turn away, yet faithfully completes his work and entrusts them to God. Ferguson observes that Moses' clear-eyed realism about human sin is matched only by God's gracious provision of a witness that will outlast it. Moses finishes his task with integrity, depositing the word and reciting the song, leaving behind a testimony to God's faithfulness that no apostasy could erase. The faithful servant completes his work and commits his rebellious people to the faithful God, whose word will accomplish his purposes even through the failures of his people.

31.theology:
God's faithful presence is the ground of courage. “Be strong and courageous… for it is the LORD your God who goes with you. He will not leave you or forsake you” (31:6, 8). Biblical courage is God-confidence, not self-confidence. The promise reverberates to every believer (Heb 13:5–6) and is fulfilled in Christ, Immanuel, who pledged, “I am with you always” (Matt 28:20).

The written, preserved, proclaimed Word. Moses writes the law, deposits it beside the ark, and commands its public reading every seventh year so every generation — including children and sojourners — may “hear and learn to fear the LORD” (31:11–13). Scripture is God's enduring, authoritative witness, the means by which faith is passed from generation to generation (Rom 10:17; 1 Tim 4:13).

God's foreknowledge and grace. God foretells Israel's apostasy before they enter the land (31:16), yet covenants with them still and provides, in advance, the Song as a witness to recall them. The God who foreknew the full depth of our sin set his love on us anyway and provided in Christ the remedy for the very unfaithfulness he foresaw.
31.examples:
Then: The aged Moses prepared to die — commissioning Joshua, charging Israel to be strong and courageous because God goes with them, depositing the written law beside the ark for public reading every seven years, and faithfully completing his work even as God foretold the people's coming apostasy and provided the Song as a witness.

Now: We face every fear and uncertain future on the same unshakable ground: the Lord himself goes with us and will never leave us nor forsake us, for Christ is Immanuel, with us always. We treasure the written, preserved, publicly proclaimed Word as the means by which faith is passed to our children. And we marvel that the God who foreknew the full depth of our sin loved us still and provided in Christ the remedy for the very unfaithfulness he foresaw — finishing his work of grace where every human leader falls short.

32.title: The Song of Moses: The Rock, His Work Is Perfect
32.text: <sup>4</sup>‘The Rock, his work is perfect, for all his ways are justice. A God of faithfulness and without iniquity, just and upright is he.’ <sup>10</sup>‘He found him in a desert land... he encircled him, he cared for him, he kept him as the apple of his eye.’ <sup>35</sup>‘Vengeance is mine, and recompense...’
32.overview:
Chapter 32 is the Song of Moses — a magnificent poetic masterpiece that rehearses the whole drama of God's faithfulness and Israel's unfaithfulness. Commanded by God as a witness (ch. 31), the song was to be learned by heart and sung in Israel, so that even in their apostasy the truth of God's character and their own failure would remain on their lips.

The song opens by exalting God as “the Rock, his work is perfect, for all his ways are justice” (32:4) — a refrain that anchors the whole poem in the unchanging faithfulness and righteousness of God. Against this backdrop, Israel's rebellion appears all the more shameful: “they have dealt corruptly with him… a crooked and twisted generation” (32:5).

The song tenderly recalls God's care for Israel in the wilderness: “He found him in a desert land… he encircled him, he cared for him, he kept him as the apple of his eye” (32:10) — one of the most beautiful images of God's love in all Scripture. Yet Israel, grown fat and prosperous, “forsook God who made him and scoffed at the Rock of his salvation” (32:15).

The song moves through judgment and the great declaration, “Vengeance is mine, and recompense” (32:35), which Paul and Hebrews both quote. Yet it ends with hope: God will have compassion on his people and atone for his land (32:43). Revelation 15:3 reveals the ultimate fulfillment — the redeemed in glory sing “the song of Moses… and the song of the Lamb,” celebrating the final exodus victory of God over all his enemies.

sections.title: The Rock, His Work Is Perfect
sections.commentary:
The song opens by calling heaven and earth to listen, and then ascribes greatness to God: “For I will proclaim the name of the LORD; ascribe greatness to our God! The Rock, his work is perfect, for all his ways are justice. A God of faithfulness and without iniquity, just and upright is he” (vv. 3–4). This is the great foundational confession of the whole song. God is “the Rock” — unchanging, immovable, utterly reliable. His work is perfect, his ways are all justice, he is faithful and without iniquity.

Sproul cherished this verse as one of the great statements of God's character in Scripture. The title “the Rock” (which recurs throughout the song) speaks of God's stability, permanence, and trustworthiness — he is the one secure foundation in a shifting world. And the affirmation that “his work is perfect” and “all his ways are justice” anchors the entire song: whatever happens, whatever judgment falls, God's character remains perfect and his justice unimpeachable. Calvin notes that this confession is set first precisely so that, when the song recounts Israel's sin and God's judgment, none can charge God with injustice; the fault lies entirely with the people.

Against this perfect Rock, Israel's corruption is exposed: “They have dealt corruptly with him; they are no longer his children because they are blemished; they are a crooked and twisted generation” (v. 5). The contrast is devastating — the perfect God and the perverse people. Begg observes the searching question that follows: “Do you thus repay the LORD, you foolish and senseless people? Is not he your father, who created you?” (v. 6). The God who is the faithful Rock is also the Father who made and redeemed them, and their rebellion is the basest ingratitude. For the believer, this verse is a refuge: in every trial and every mystery, we rest on the Rock whose work is perfect and whose ways are all justice. When we cannot trace his hand, we trust his character; the Rock does not move.

sections.title: The Apple of His Eye: God's Tender Care
sections.commentary:
The song now rehearses God's gracious dealings with Israel, and it rises to some of the tenderest imagery in all of Scripture. “He found him in a desert land, and in the howling waste of the wilderness; he encircled him, he cared for him, he kept him as the apple of his eye” (v. 10). To be “the apple of his eye” is to be the cherished pupil of the eye — the most precious, most protected, most instinctively guarded part of the body. God watched over Israel with this kind of jealous tenderness.

The imagery intensifies: “Like an eagle that stirs up its nest, that flutters over its young, spreading out its wings, catching them, bearing them on its pinions, the LORD alone guided him” (vv. 11–12). The picture is of a mother eagle teaching her young to fly, hovering beneath them, ready to catch them on her wings if they falter. So God bore Israel through the wilderness, guiding, protecting, sustaining. Begg savors this image of divine tenderness — the strength of the eagle joined to the care of a mother, the God who bears his stumbling children on his wings. Sproul noted that these images reveal the heart of God toward his people: not cold sovereignty but warm, watchful, fatherly love.

And God's care brought abundance: he made Israel “ride on the high places of the land,” feeding him with the produce of the field, honey from the rock, oil from the flinty crag, the finest of wheat and wine (vv. 13–14). The God who found Israel in the howling waste brought them into a land of abundance, lavishing good upon them. Ferguson notes the deliberate contrast being set up: this tender care and lavish provision make Israel's coming ingratitude all the more shameful. For the believer, these verses are a portrait of the love of God for his own — he finds us in the wilderness of our lostness, encircles us, keeps us as the apple of his eye, and bears us on eagle's wings through every trial, lavishing his grace upon us. We are precious to him beyond telling, guarded with a jealous, fatherly love.

sections.title: Jeshurun Grew Fat: Forsaking the Rock
sections.commentary:
Now the song turns dark with the tragedy of ingratitude: “But Jeshurun grew fat, and kicked… then he forsook God who made him and scoffed at the Rock of his salvation” (v. 15). “Jeshurun” is an affectionate name for Israel (“the upright one”), making the betrayal all the more poignant. Grown fat and prosperous on God's abundance, Israel kicked against their benefactor like a well-fed animal, forsaking the very Rock that had saved them. Here the peril of prosperity (ch. 8) comes to its bitter fruition. Begg notes the searing diagnosis: it was abundance, not affliction, that turned Israel away; full and comfortable, they forgot the God who fed them.

They turned to idols — “strange gods,” “new gods that had come recently” — and “sacrificed to demons that were no gods” (vv. 16–17). Sproul stressed the staggering folly: they exchanged the eternal Rock for newfangled nothings, the faithful God for lifeless demons. And God's response is grief and judgment: “I will hide my face from them; I will see what their end will be” (v. 20). He would provoke them to jealousy by “those who are no people” (v. 21) — a verse Paul quotes (Rom 10:19) to explain how God turned to the Gentiles to provoke Israel to jealousy.

The song depicts the fierceness of God's judgment against persistent rebellion — fire, famine, sword, and terror (vv. 22–25). Yet even here, restraint appears: God would not utterly destroy them, lest the enemy boast, “Our hand is triumphant, it was not the LORD who did all this” (v. 27). Calvin notes that God tempers his judgment for the sake of his own glory and his covenant. Ferguson observes the relentless contrast between the perfect Rock and the perverse people, between God's faithfulness and Israel's treachery. The song forces Israel — and us — to face the depth of human ingratitude and the holiness of the God who will not be mocked. The folly of forsaking the Rock of salvation for the broken cisterns of idolatry stands exposed in all its tragedy.

sections.title: Vengeance Is Mine; the Song of Moses and the Lamb
sections.commentary:
The song moves toward its climax with the great declaration of God's justice: “Vengeance is mine, and recompense, for the time when their foot shall slip” (v. 35). This verse is quoted twice in the New Testament — by Paul (Rom 12:19), who uses it to forbid personal vengeance (“never avenge yourselves… for it is written, ‘Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord'”), and by the writer of Hebrews (Heb 10:30) as a warning of God's judgment. Sproul stressed the comfort and the warning in this verse: vengeance belongs to God alone, who will perfectly recompense all wrong; we need not avenge ourselves, for the righteous Judge will settle every account.

Then comes the great affirmation of God's sole sovereignty: “See now that I, even I, am he, and there is no god beside me; I kill and I make alive; I wound and I heal; and there is none that can deliver out of my hand” (v. 39). This is one of the most majestic statements of God's absolute sovereignty in all of Scripture — over life and death, wounding and healing, with none able to deliver from his hand. Calvin saw here the comprehensive lordship of God over all things.

And the song ends not in judgment but in hope: “Rejoice with him, O heavens; bow down to him, all gods… for he avenges the blood of his children and… atones for his land, his people” (v. 43). The God who judges also redeems; he will atone for his people. The ultimate fulfillment is breathtaking: in Revelation 15:3, the redeemed in glory, victorious over the beast, sing “the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb” — the song of the final exodus, the great deliverance accomplished by Christ. Ferguson notes the glorious convergence: the song that witnessed against Israel's sin becomes, in Christ, the song of the redeemed celebrating God's triumph. The chapter closes with God's command for Moses to ascend Mount Nebo to die (vv. 48–52), the law-giver who could not enter the land — pointing once more to the One who would do what Moses could not. The Rock whose work is perfect has secured the final victory, and his redeemed people will sing the song of Moses and the Lamb forever.

32.theology:
The Rock whose work is perfect. “The Rock, his work is perfect, for all his ways are justice” (32:4). God is the unchanging, faithful, righteous foundation; his character anchors the whole song. When we cannot trace his hand in trial or judgment, we trust his character — the Rock does not move. “I, even I, am he… I kill and I make alive… none can deliver out of my hand” (32:39).

The tender love of God and the tragedy of ingratitude. God kept Israel “as the apple of his eye,” bearing them like an eagle on its wings (32:10–11), yet “Jeshurun grew fat, and kicked… and forsook God” (32:15). Prosperity, not affliction, turned them away — the peril of abundance come to bitter fruit. God's lavish love makes ingratitude the basest folly.

Vengeance belongs to God; the song of Moses and the Lamb. “Vengeance is mine, and recompense” (32:35; cf. Rom 12:19; Heb 10:30) — the righteous Judge will settle every account. Yet the song ends in hope: God atones for his people (32:43). In Revelation 15:3 the redeemed sing “the song of Moses… and the song of the Lamb,” celebrating the final exodus victory secured by Christ.
32.examples:
Then: Moses gave Israel a song to learn by heart — exalting the Rock whose work is perfect, recalling God's tender care that kept them as the apple of his eye and bore them on eagle's wings, exposing the tragedy of a prosperous people forsaking their Rock, and declaring that vengeance and final atonement belong to God alone.

Now: We rest on the Rock whose work is perfect, trusting his character when we cannot trace his hand; we marvel that he found us in the wilderness of our lostness and keeps us as the apple of his eye, bearing us on his wings; we guard against the prosperity that breeds ingratitude; and we leave all vengeance to the righteous Judge. And one day, victorious in Christ, we will join the redeemed of every age to sing the song of Moses and the song of the Lamb, celebrating the final exodus victory of our God forever.

33.title: The Blessing of Moses: The Eternal God Is Your Dwelling Place
33.text: <sup>26</sup>‘There is none like God, O Jeshurun, who rides through the heavens to your help, through the skies in his majesty. <sup>27</sup>The eternal God is your dwelling place, and underneath are the everlasting arms.’ <sup>29</sup>‘Happy are you, O Israel! Who is like you, a people saved by the LORD...’
33.overview:
Chapter 33 is the Blessing of Moses — the last words of the great prophet, spoken over the tribes of Israel before his death, in the manner of Jacob's blessing over his sons (Gen 49). Having sung the song of God's faithfulness and Israel's failure, Moses now blesses each tribe, looking forward in hope to their life in the land under the care of their God.

The chapter opens with a majestic poetic prologue celebrating the LORD's appearance at Sinai and his kingship over “Jeshurun” (Israel) — “he was king in Jeshurun” (33:5). Then Moses pronounces blessings on the tribes one by one — Reuben, Judah, Levi, Benjamin, Joseph, Zebulun, Gad, Dan, Naphtali, Asher — each blessing tailored to the tribe's character and calling.

The chapter rises to a glorious crescendo in its closing verses, among the most comforting in all of Scripture: “There is none like God, O Jeshurun, who rides through the heavens to your help… The eternal God is your dwelling place, and underneath are the everlasting arms” (33:26–27). Here the incomparable, majestic God is also the believer's secure dwelling and unfailing support.

Moses ends with a benediction of joy: “Happy are you, O Israel! Who is like you, a people saved by the LORD, the shield of your help, and the sword of your triumph!” (33:29). The dying prophet's last word over his people is not curse but blessing, not despair but joy — a people saved by the LORD. For the believer, these closing words are a treasure: the eternal God is our dwelling place, and underneath are the everlasting arms.

sections.title: The LORD King in Jeshurun: The Majestic Prologue
sections.commentary:
Moses, “the man of God,” begins his final blessing with a majestic poetic prologue. He recalls the LORD's glorious appearance at Sinai: “The LORD came from Sinai and dawned from Seir upon us; he shone forth from Mount Paran; he came from the ten thousands of holy ones” (v. 2). The God who blesses his people is the God of awesome majesty, attended by myriads of holy ones, blazing forth in glory. Calvin notes that Moses sets the blessing within the context of God's revealed majesty and his love for his people — “yes, he loved his people, all his holy ones were in his hand” (v. 3).

The prologue holds together two truths that run through all of Scripture: God's transcendent majesty and his intimate love. He shines forth in blazing glory, yet “he loved his people” and holds his holy ones “in his hand.” Begg observes the beautiful tension — the God of overwhelming majesty is the God of tender love, the One before whom the holy ones tremble is the One who cradles his people in his hand. Sproul stressed that this is the God of the Bible: infinitely exalted and yet intimately near, holy beyond comprehension and yet loving beyond measure.

And the prologue declares God's kingship: “he was king in Jeshurun, when the heads of the people were gathered” (v. 5). The LORD himself is Israel's true King. Before any earthly monarch, before the request for a king “like the nations” (ch. 17), the LORD reigns over his people. Ferguson notes that this kingship of God is the foundation of Israel's identity and security; they are the people of the great King. For the believer, this prologue sets the tone for all the blessings that follow — every blessing flows from the majestic, loving, reigning God who has made his people his own. The God who came from Sinai in blazing glory loves his people and holds them in his hand, and he reigns as King over all who are his.

sections.title: Blessings on the Tribes: Each According to Its Calling
sections.commentary:
Moses now blesses the tribes one by one, each blessing fitted to the tribe's character and calling. Reuben is preserved though diminished (v. 6). Judah is granted strength and the prayer that God would bring him to his people — a tribe destined for kingship and, ultimately, for the Messiah (v. 7). Levi receives an extended blessing, honored for faithfulness and entrusted with teaching God's law and offering the sacrifices: “They shall teach Jacob your rules and Israel your law; they shall put incense before you” (vv. 8–11). Levi, who had no land but had the LORD as their inheritance, is given the priestly ministry of the word and the altar.

Benjamin is called “the beloved of the LORD,” who dwells in safety, for “the High God surrounds him all day long, and dwells between his shoulders” (v. 12) — a tender image of God carrying his beloved like a child borne on the shoulders. Begg savors this picture of security and intimacy: to be the beloved of the LORD, surrounded and carried by him all day long. Then Joseph receives the richest blessing of all — the choicest gifts of heaven and earth, the favor of “him who dwells in the bush,” abundance and strength and might (vv. 13–17).

Sproul observed that these tailored blessings reflect God's particular care for each part of his people; God does not deal with his people as an undifferentiated mass but knows and provides for each according to its calling and need. Calvin notes that the variety of blessings reflects the variety of gifts and roles within the one people of God. Ferguson connects this to the New Testament vision of the body of Christ, in which each member has its own gift and calling, and God provides for each (1 Cor 12; Rom 12). The God who blessed each tribe according to its calling is the God who gives to each of his children their particular gifts, callings, and provisions. None is overlooked; each is known, blessed, and provided for by the God who reigns as King over his people and loves them each by name.

sections.title: The Remaining Tribes Blessed
sections.commentary:
Moses continues blessing the remaining tribes. Zebulun and Issachar are blessed in their going out and their tents, drawing wealth from the seas and the sand (vv. 18–19). Gad is blessed with enlargement and strength, dwelling like a lion (vv. 20–21). Dan is “a lion's cub” (v. 22). Naphtali is “sated with favor, and full of the blessing of the LORD,” possessing the lake and the south (v. 23). Asher is blessed most abundantly with sons, favor, oil, and security: “Let him dip his foot in oil. Your bars shall be iron and bronze, and as your days, so shall your strength be” (vv. 24–25).

That final phrase to Asher — “as your days, so shall your strength be” (v. 25) — has become a treasured promise for believers in every age. It assures that God will supply strength proportioned to each day's need; whatever the demands of the day, God's grace will be sufficient. Begg loves to apply this pastorally: we are not given strength for tomorrow's burdens today, but we are promised strength equal to each day as it comes. God's mercies are “new every morning” (Lam 3:23), and his grace is sufficient for every day's trial. Paul echoes the same comfort: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Cor 12:9).

Sproul stressed the daily, proportioned nature of God's provision — we live by faith one day at a time, trusting God to supply strength as each day requires. This is the manna principle: gathered fresh each morning, sufficient for the day. Ferguson notes the comfort for the weak and weary: God does not overwhelm us with the strength for a lifetime all at once, but faithfully provides what each day demands. The believer facing daunting trials can rest in this promise: “as your days, so shall your strength be.” Whatever the day holds, the strength will be there, supplied fresh by the God who knows our frame and proportions his grace to our need. We need not fear tomorrow, for tomorrow's strength will come with tomorrow, from the unfailing hand of our faithful God.

sections.title: The Eternal God Is Your Dwelling Place
sections.commentary:
The blessing rises to a glorious crescendo in verses that rank among the most comforting in all of Scripture. “There is none like God, O Jeshurun, who rides through the heavens to your help, through the skies in his majesty. The eternal God is your dwelling place, and underneath are the everlasting arms” (vv. 26–27). Here the incomparable, majestic God — who rides the heavens in his glory — is also the believer's secure dwelling and unfailing support.

“The eternal God is your dwelling place.” Sproul cherished this truth: our true home is not a place but a Person; the eternal God himself is the dwelling in which we are safe and at rest. As the psalmist sang, “Lord, you have been our dwelling place in all generations” (Ps 90:1, also written by Moses). Whatever happens to our earthly dwellings, the eternal God remains our secure and unchanging home. Begg observes the comfort: we dwell not in a fragile shelter but in the eternal God, who can never be shaken or destroyed.

“And underneath are the everlasting arms.” This is one of the tenderest images in all Scripture. Beneath all our weakness, our falling, our fear, are the everlasting arms of God — arms that never tire, never weaken, never let go. When we sink, they bear us up; when we fall, they catch us; when we are weak, they hold us fast. Ferguson notes the layered comfort: above us the God who rides the heavens to our help, beneath us the everlasting arms that never fail. We are enclosed, surrounded, upheld by the eternal God. And Moses ends with joy: “Happy are you, O Israel! Who is like you, a people saved by the LORD, the shield of your help, and the sword of your triumph!” (v. 29). The dying prophet's last word over his people is not curse but blessing, not despair but joy — a people saved by the LORD. For the believer, these closing words are a treasure beyond price: the eternal God is our dwelling place, the everlasting arms are underneath us, and we are a people saved by the LORD. There is none like our God.

33.theology:
The eternal God is our dwelling place. “The eternal God is your dwelling place, and underneath are the everlasting arms” (33:27). Our true home is not a place but a Person; the eternal God is our secure, unchanging refuge (cf. Ps 90:1). Beneath all our weakness and falling are the everlasting arms that never tire and never let go. There is none like our God (33:26).

God's majesty and intimate love. The God who “rides through the heavens… in his majesty” (33:26) is the God who “loved his people” and holds his holy ones “in his hand” (33:3), carrying his beloved on his shoulders (33:12). Transcendent majesty and tender, intimate love meet in the God who reigns as King over his people (33:5).

Strength proportioned to each day. “As your days, so shall your strength be” (33:25). God supplies grace sufficient for each day's need — the manna principle, mercies new every morning (Lam 3:23; 2 Cor 12:9). We need not fear tomorrow, for tomorrow's strength will come with tomorrow from the unfailing hand of God.
33.examples:
