Then: The dying Moses blessed the tribes of Israel one by one, each according to its calling, exalting the LORD as their majestic King and tender Father, promising strength proportioned to each day, and crowning his last words with the glorious assurance that the eternal God is their dwelling place and underneath are the everlasting arms.

Now: We rest in the same incomparable God — our true home not a fragile place but the eternal God himself, who upholds us with everlasting arms beneath every weakness and fall. We trust his grace to be sufficient for each day as it comes, never fearing tomorrow. And we rejoice with Moses' last blessing: happy are we, a people saved by the LORD, dwelling in the eternal God, carried in his arms, loved and reigned over by the King of heaven. There is none like our God.

34.title: The Death of Moses: The Law Could Not Bring Them In
34.text: <sup>5</sup>So Moses the servant of the LORD died there in the land of Moab, according to the word of the LORD. <sup>10</sup>And there has not arisen a prophet since in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face.
34.overview:
Chapter 34 brings Deuteronomy — and the entire Pentateuch — to its solemn and poignant close: the death of Moses. The greatest prophet Israel had ever known climbs Mount Nebo, sees the Promised Land spread out before him, and dies there in the land of Moab, never having set foot in Canaan. God himself buries him in an unknown grave, and Israel mourns for thirty days.

The scene is heavy with significance. Moses, the mediator of the old covenant, the law-giver, the man who led Israel out of Egypt and through forty years of wilderness, cannot bring the people into the inheritance. He can only see it from afar. The law shows us the land; it cannot carry us across the Jordan. This is the great theological climax toward which the whole book has pointed.

Joshua — whose name is Yeshua, the Hebrew name behind Jesus — is now “full of the spirit of wisdom” and takes up the leadership. He will do what Moses could not: lead the people into the land. The law cannot save; only the Savior can bring us into the inheritance.

The book closes with a tribute to Moses' unique greatness: “there has not arisen a prophet since in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face” (34:10). Yet the very greatness of Moses, and his inability to enter the land, point beyond him to the Prophet greater than Moses (18:15) — to Christ, who not only sees the land but brings his people home, the One whom God knew not merely face to face but as the eternal Son.

sections.title: Moses Sees the Land from Pisgah
sections.commentary:
Moses climbs Mount Nebo, to the top of Pisgah, and the LORD shows him the whole land — Gilead, Dan, Naphtali, Ephraim, Manasseh, Judah, the Negeb, the plain of Jericho — the entire sweep of the inheritance promised to the fathers. “And the LORD said to him, ‘This is the land of which I swore to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob… I have let you see it with your eyes, but you shall not go over there'” (v. 4).

It is a poignant scene of mingled grace and discipline. In grace, God grants Moses the sight of the land he had labored forty years to reach — the LORD himself shows it to him, spread out in its fullness. Yet the old word stands: “you shall not go over there.” Moses sees but does not enter. Begg notes the tender mercy even in the denial — God does not leave Moses to die without a glimpse of the goal, but personally shows him the land, as if to say, “The promise is sure; you have seen it with your own eyes.”

Sproul reflected on the deep theological weight of this moment: Moses, the embodiment of the law, the mediator of the old covenant, is permitted to see the land but not to enter it. The denial traces back to his sin at Meribah (Num 20), reminding us that even the greatest saints fall short and that God's holiness is not to be trifled with. But there is a profounder truth here. Ferguson observes that it was fitting that Moses, who represents the law, should not bring the people into the rest, for the law cannot bring anyone into the inheritance. Moses on Pisgah, gazing at the land he will never enter, is a figure of the law itself — glorious, faithful, yet unable to save. He can show us the promise; he cannot carry us across the Jordan. The law brings us to the very border of rest and reveals the inheritance, but only Another can bring us in.

sections.title: The Death and Burial of Moses
sections.commentary:
“So Moses the servant of the LORD died there in the land of Moab, according to the word of the LORD. And he buried him in the valley in the land of Moab… but no one knows the place of his burial to this day” (vv. 5–6). The greatest prophet of the old covenant dies in Moab, outside the land, and God himself buries him in a grave no one would ever find. He was a hundred and twenty years old, “his eye was undimmed, and his vigor unabated” (v. 7) — he did not die of weakness but at the appointed word of God.

The title given to Moses here is profound: “Moses the servant of the LORD.” For all his greatness, his deepest identity was that of a servant — one who faithfully did his Master's will. Calvin notes the dignity of this title; there is no higher honor than to be called the servant of the LORD, and Moses bore it to the end. He died “according to the word of the LORD” — the Hebrew phrase suggests “at the mouth of the LORD,” which Jewish tradition tenderly rendered as dying by the kiss of God. Even in death, Moses was in the LORD's hands.

That God himself buried Moses, in a secret grave, is striking. Sproul observed that this prevented Moses' tomb from becoming a shrine or object of idolatrous veneration; the focus must remain on God, not on his servant. The secret grave guards against the human tendency to worship the messenger rather than the One who sent him. Interestingly, the body of Moses is mentioned again in Jude 9, where the archangel Michael disputes with the devil over it — a glimpse into unseen realities surrounding even his death. Israel wept and mourned for Moses thirty days (v. 8). Begg notes the deep grief of a people who had been led by this man through every trial; the loss of so great a leader was rightly mourned. Yet even as they mourned, the work of God went on, for God's purposes do not die with his servants. The servant of the LORD finished his course and rested, his work complete, his grave in the hand of the God he served.

sections.title: Joshua Takes Up the Leadership
sections.commentary:
“And Joshua the son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom, for Moses had laid his hands on him. So the people of Israel obeyed him and did as the LORD had commanded Moses” (v. 9). The leadership passes from Moses to Joshua, who is equipped by the Spirit for the task and commissioned by the laying on of hands. The transition is orderly and Spirit-empowered; God does not leave his people leaderless but raises up the one prepared to bring them into the land.

Here is the theological heart of the chapter's hope, and it shines with gospel light. Moses, the law-giver, could not bring the people into the inheritance — but Joshua will. And the name Joshua is Yehoshua, shortened to Yeshua — the very name that, in Greek, becomes Iesous, Jesus. The man who does what Moses could not, who leads the people across the Jordan into the promised rest, bears the name of the Savior. Sproul and many others have delighted to trace this: the law (Moses) brings us to the border and shows us the promise, but it cannot carry us across; only Joshua-Jesus brings us in.

Ferguson draws out the rich typology: the inability of Moses and the success of Joshua dramatize the great truth of the gospel — “the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17). The law cannot save; it can only reveal the inheritance and our inability to reach it. But the One who bears the name of salvation does what the law could never do — he leads his people through the waters of death into the everlasting inheritance. Begg observes the comfort: we are not left to be brought home by the law, which can only condemn, but by Jesus, who has gone before us and brings us in. The God who equipped Joshua by his Spirit to lead Israel into Canaan is the God who has given us his Spirit and his Son to bring us into the rest that remains for the people of God. Where Moses falls silent, Joshua rises; where the law fails, Christ saves.

sections.title: There Has Not Arisen a Prophet Like Moses
sections.commentary:
The book closes with a tribute to Moses' unparalleled greatness: “And there has not arisen a prophet since in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face, none like him for all the signs and the wonders that the LORD sent him to do… and for all the mighty power and all the great deeds of terror that Moses did in the sight of all Israel” (vv. 10–12). Moses stands alone — the prophet who knew God “face to face,” who performed the signs of the exodus, who mediated the covenant. No one since had equaled him.

This is a fitting epitaph for the greatest figure of the old covenant. Yet the very statement, “there has not arisen a prophet since like Moses,” leaves the reader looking forward. For Moses himself had prophesied: “The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me… it is to him you shall listen” (18:15). The closing words of Deuteronomy, lamenting that no prophet like Moses had yet arisen, create a longing and an expectation that point beyond the old covenant to the Prophet who would come.

And that Prophet did come. The New Testament declares that Jesus is the Prophet greater than Moses (Acts 3:22–23; Heb 3:1–6). Where Moses knew God “face to face” as a servant, Jesus is the eternal Son who is “in the bosom of the Father” (John 1:18) and has made him known. Where Moses' face shone with reflected glory that faded (2 Cor 3:7), Christ is the very radiance of God's glory (Heb 1:3). Where Moses was “faithful in all God's house as a servant,” Christ is “faithful over God's house as a son” (Heb 3:5–6). Sproul stressed the surpassing greatness of Christ over Moses: as glorious as Moses was, he was but a servant pointing to the Son. Ferguson notes the deliberate open-endedness of the ending — Deuteronomy closes with a death and an unfulfilled longing, looking forward to the One who would not only see the land but bring his people in, and who would be the Prophet, Priest, and King that Moses could only foreshadow. The law-giver dies outside the land; the Savior brings us home. And so the book of remembrance and obedience ends, pointing past its greatest servant to the greater Prophet, the true Joshua, our Lord Jesus Christ, who does for us all that Moses could not — and brings us, at last, into the rest of God.

34.theology:
The law cannot bring us in; only the Savior can. Moses, the law-giver and mediator of the old covenant, sees the land but cannot enter it (34:4). The law shows us the inheritance and our inability to reach it, but it cannot carry us across the Jordan. Only Joshua — Yeshua, Jesus — leads the people in (34:9), for “the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17). Where the law fails, Christ saves.

The servant of the LORD. Moses' deepest identity, even in death, was “the servant of the LORD” (34:5), faithful to the end. God himself buried him in a secret grave, guarding against idolatry of the messenger and keeping the focus on the One who sent him. The faithful servant finished his course; God's purposes did not die with him.

The Prophet greater than Moses. “There has not arisen a prophet since in Israel like Moses” (34:10) — yet Moses himself foretold the Prophet to come (18:15). The book ends in longing, pointing to Jesus, the eternal Son, faithful over God's house as a Son (Heb 3:5–6), the radiance of God's glory (Heb 1:3), who is everything Moses foreshadowed and infinitely more.
34.examples:
Then: Moses, the greatest prophet of the old covenant, climbed Mount Nebo, saw the Promised Land he could never enter, and died as the servant of the LORD in Moab, buried by God in a secret grave — while Joshua, full of the Spirit, took up the leadership to bring Israel into the land Moses could not.

Now: We see in the death of Moses the great truth of the gospel: the law brings us to the border and shows us the promise, but it cannot carry us home; only Jesus — the true Joshua, the Prophet greater than Moses — leads his people through the waters of death into the everlasting inheritance. Where the law-giver falls silent, the Savior rises. And so Deuteronomy, the book of remembering and obeying, ends by pointing past its greatest servant to the greater Prophet, our Lord Jesus Christ, who does for us all that Moses could not, and brings us at last into the rest of God.
